articles.body: PIMPRI CHINCHWAD: Shiv Sena (UBT) has announced a reward of Rs 71,000 for anyone who slaps Shiv Sena leader Shaina NC, escalating the political row over an incident involving a photograph of party founder Balasaheb Thackeray.Making the announcement on Thursday, Shiv Sena (UBT)'s Pimpri Chinchwad unit president Chetan Pawar told reporters that the reward was being offered in response to a similar announcement by a Shiv Sena (UBT) office-bearer from Mumbai."As everyone knows, our party office-bearer from Mumbai has already announced a reward of Rs 1 lakh for anyone who slaps Shaina NC. Similarly, we, as the Pimpri Chinchwad unit of Shiv Sena (UBT), announce a reward of Rs 71,000 for anyone who slaps her," Pawar said.Row over Balasaheb Thackeray's photographThe controversy erupted on Wednesday during a press conference organised by the Shinde-led Shiv Sena in Mumbai to protest against references to Hindutva ideologue V D Savarkar in Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love.During the protest, party leaders tore pages from the book. Shaina was also seen tearing a portion of a photograph depicting Balasaheb Thackeray striking an effigy of Congress leader Mani Shankar Aiyar with a slipper. The incident was captured on camera and drew criticism from Shiv Sena (UBT) leaders.Shaina denied deliberately disrespecting Balasaheb, maintaining that she had torn the portion showing Aiyar and not the photograph of the late Shiv Sena founder. Maharashtra deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde also defended her explanation.On Thursday, Shaina apologised to Balasaheb's admirers if her actions had hurt their sentiments, while insisting that she had no intention of disrespecting him.The incident has triggered a fresh confrontation between the rival Shiv Sena factions led by Uddhav Thackeray and Eknath Shinde.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says US may reverse its immigration curbs: ‘ Given the scale of MAGA losses, it is likely…’
articles.summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu believes the US could see a sharp reversal in its immigration policies following political setbacks for the Make America Great
articles.body: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu believes the US could see a sharp reversal in its immigration policies following political setbacks for the Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Vembu suggested that the change could affect both legal and illegal immigration, potentially bringing back population-driven demand that had slowed during recent years. Vembu also linked immigration to the US housing market, saying immigrants had been an important source of housing demand.“Given the scale of MAGA losses, it is likely that immigration policy will make a sharp reversal in America, both legal and illegal immigration,” Sridhar Vembu wrote.Vembu said the US economy had long been supported by what he called "demographic fuel". He used the housing market as an example, explaining that immigrants contributed to demand for homes and rental properties.“The unsustainable financial and economic bubble had long been sustained with demographic fuel,” he said adding “A good example is housing. Housing demand at the margin came from immigrants and that demand got sharply cut in recent MAGA years”.By demographic fuel, Vembu seems to be referring to the demand created by population growth. As more people move into a country, the need for housing and other goods and services also increases.What Sridhar Vembu expects from a possible immigration policy reversalSridhar Vembu said tighter immigration rules had temporarily reduced a source of demand that had supported the economy. If the policies change, this demand could return."The demographic fuel tap for the bubble was shut for a period and now it may be turned back on," he wrote. However, Vembu clarified that he was not making a definite prediction about the future of US immigration policy."Not a prediction so much as a possible scenario to keep in mind," he added.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Bengaluru man buys Rs 479 chocolate gift pack from Blinkit, finds 3 of 6 chocolates expired 2 months earlier; consumer forum holds Blinkit guilty of deficiency in service, orders Rs 479 refund, Rs 3,000 compensation and Rs 40,000 punitive damages
articles.summary: BENGALURU: The chocolates tasted off, and when a 30-year-old finally read the wrappers, he understood why.
articles.body: BENGALURU: The chocolates tasted off, and when a 30-year-old finally read the wrappers, he understood why. Half the gift box he had ordered for Valentine's Day had expired two months before it reached his doorstep. Now, quick-commerce platform Blinkit must pay far more than the Rs 479 he spent after the Bangalore Urban IV Additional District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission held it guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.The saga began on February 14, 2026, when Manju Prasad K, a resident of Hegganahalli Cross, ordered a Choco Cart Chocolate Gift Pack (Grand) through the Blinkit app. He paid Rs 479 through UPI, comprising Rs 469 for the product and Rs 10 in handling charges. The pack, weighing 223.5 grams and containing six varieties of chocolates, arrived in about 20 minutes.Over the next five days, he ate the chocolates. On February 21, he noticed a change in their taste and checked the individual wrappers. He found that three of the six chocolates had expired on December 14, 2025, while the other three were close to their expiry dates.He immediately complained to Blinkit's help desk and followed up with an email on February 28. The company replied that complaints had to be raised within seven days of delivery and that it could not process a refund or replacement. Prasad approached the commission on March 23, seeking a refund of Rs 479, compensation of Rs 25 lakh and Rs 15,000 towards litigation and travel expenses.In their defence, Blinkit and Blink Commerce Pvt Ltd argued that the product page carried a return policy allowing replacements only within 72 hours of delivery and that the complaint had been filed after this period. They also contended that his consumption of the chocolates over five days had deprived them of an opportunity to verify the product. Further, they argued that the expiry dates on individual wrappers did not establish that the entire pack was expired or unfit for consumption. Pointing to the absence of medical records, prescriptions or bills, they said no injury had been demonstrated and sought dismissal of the complaint with exemplary costs.The commission noted that the companies had cited both a seven-day and a 72-hour limit, positions it found contradictory. It observed that the box had been delivered at around 11.45 pm, making it impossible for the complainant to consume all six varieties on the same day. It therefore held that the February 21 complaint was filed within seven days of delivery. It also pointed out that the original wrappers had been produced before it and that the companies had not specifically denied supplying expired chocolates, but had primarily disputed the complaint on the ground of delay.The commission observed: “It is not the question of replacement of the chocolate box or refund of the amount, as a seller should not keep expired edible things in the shop.” It described the practice of packing good and expired chocolates in the same gift box as “highly condemnable”. It also accepted Prasad's argument that this was done around Christmas and Valentine's Day, when buyers might not check the expiry dates. The commission noted that Blinkit's counsel had not objected to this submission.Calling it a matter of public health, the commission said many people in cities such as Bengaluru depended on online platforms and that taking advantage of their trust was unfair.Holding that the companies had supplied expired chocolates despite knowing that they had expired two months before delivery, the commission found them guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. The bench, comprising president Vijaykumar M Pawale, member Chandrashekar S Noola and lady member K Anita Shivakumar, partly allowed the complaint on November 6.In the order authored by K Anita Shivakumar, the commission directed both companies to jointly refund Rs 479 and pay Rs 3,000 as compensation for mental agony and hardship. articles.summary: The cost of the US war against Iran has reached an estimated $48.3 billion, excluding the damage to American military bases in West Asia hit by Iranian
articles.body: The cost of the US war against Iran has reached an estimated $48.3 billion, excluding the damage to American military bases in West Asia hit by Iranian attacks. Lawmakers on Thursday pressed the Pentagon to provide a separate assessment of the losses suffered by US installations.The latest cost estimate, dated November 13, was announced on Thursday by Pentagon budget official Arthur Miller, as he appeared before the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering his nomination as Navy comptroller.The estimate covers military operations and the replacement of equipment and munitions.Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut asked Miller how much damage had been caused to US military installations. Miller said he did not have an estimate. Committee chairman and Republican Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi directed him to try to provide the figures as soon as possible, the Associated Press reported.The war's financial cost has become a point of contention in Congress, with the debate intensifying as the Trump administration seeks approval for a $1.5 trillion defence budget. The conflict and its economic consequences contributed to heavy Republican losses in the midterm elections. Financial scrutiny of the war is expected to intensify when Democrats take control of Congress in January for the remainder of President Donald Trump's term.According to an analysis by the Associated Press, Iranian attacks had damaged aircraft hangars, systems used to detect incoming strikes, warehouses, troop accommodation and other facilities, resulting in billions of dollars in equipment losses.The Pentagon has faced mounting pressure from Democrats to disclose the extent of damage to American bases across the Middle East following Iranian missile and drone attacks.At a confirmation hearing on Tuesday, senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts questioned acting navy secretary Hung Cao over the financial impact of the war as he sought confirmation for the permanent post.Citing independent estimates and media reports, Warren said the US naval blockade of Iranian shipping was costing about $32.5 million a day, while an Iranian attack on the Navy's regional headquarters in Bahrain had caused at least $400 million in damage.Cao confirmed the daily cost of the blockade but said he could not provide a comprehensive assessment of the damage in Bahrain because "it's a nonpermissive area for us to go". Months earlier, Cao had told a reporter that Iran "blew the hell" out of Bahrain.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US to announce cause of nationwide FAA outage that disrupted 18,000 flights
articles.summary: The US government is expected to announce this week the root cause of a router outage that triggered a nationwide aviation ground stop on November 13,
articles.body: The US government is expected to announce this week the root cause of a router outage that triggered a nationwide aviation ground stop on November 13, Federal Aviation Administration chief Bryan Bedford said on Thursday.The disruption affected more than 18,000 flights and over one million passengers. It was the longest nationwide aviation ground stop in the US since the September 11, 2001, attacks, Reuters reported.Bedford declined to discuss the findings, saying transportation secretary Sean Duffy would brief the public on the investigation's outcome.Duffy has said a Juniper router installed by L3Harris Technologies at a remote facility in Arkansas triggered the nearly five-hour shutdown. Bedford said the Federal Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network, operated by L3Harris since 2002, was in urgent need of replacement.“We have a patchwork, archaic federal telephone network, which is why we've got to get off of it as fast as humanly possible while maintaining safety,” he said.On Wednesday, Duffy said that the team responsible for monitoring the network played a critical role and that the outage had not been identified quickly enough.As per Reuters, the transportation secretary said 68 routers previously installed by Juniper Networks, which is owned by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, had not caused any problems. However, the FAA has suspended further installations while testing continues at an L3Harris laboratory in Florida, with the FAA, Cisco and the FBI involved.Duffy has also urged Congress to approve an additional $50 billion to complete major upgrades to the ageing US air traffic control system and airports. Lawmakers had approved $12.5 billion for the upgrades last year, although some legislators favour a smaller allocation focused specifically on safety improvements.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bengaluru man borrows money for pilot training, pays academy Rs 10 lakh, it fails to start commercial flying course for over 2 years, consumer commission orders Rs 10 lakh refund with 6% interest and Rs 20,000 compensation
articles.summary: BENGALURU: A Bengaluru consumer commission has directed the Indian Flying Academy to refund Rs 10 lakh collected from a 25-year-old aspiring pilot after
articles.body: BENGALURU: A Bengaluru consumer commission has directed the Indian Flying Academy to refund Rs 10 lakh collected from a 25-year-old aspiring pilot after it failed to commence a commercial pilot licence (CPL) training programme despite collecting the admission fee and repeatedly postponing the start of classes for more than two years.The Bengaluru Urban District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission also ordered the academy to pay Rs 10,000 as compensation for mental agony and another Rs 10,000 towards litigation expenses. The refund will carry 6% annual interest from the respective dates of payment until realisation.Aaron Antony, a resident of Yelahanka, had enrolled in the academy's CPL programme for the 2023-25 training period. According to his complaint, the academy quoted a total course fee of Rs 40 lakh and assured him that training would begin promptly.He paid Rs 10 lakh in three instalments: Rs 50,000 and Rs 3 lakh on February 28, 2023, followed by Rs 6.5 lakh on April 5, 2023.However, the academy did not begin the programme and continued postponing its commencement on various grounds. Antony said that by the time he approached the commission, he should have completed the entire course, but his training had not even started.His parents had borrowed money at an interest rate of 2% a month to fund his admission, the complaint stated. Repeated requests and emails seeking either commencement of training or a refund did not yield a response. He subsequently sent a legal notice on February 5, 2025, demanding repayment.The academy did not appear before the commission or file its written version despite being served notice. It was placed ex parte on February 4, 2026.The commission observed that the academy's failure to respond left Antony's allegations uncontroverted. It also examined the brochure, fee structure and payment receipts issued by the academy, which established that it had collected Rs 10 lakh for the course.Holding that the academy had breached the agreed terms by neither commencing the training nor refunding the money, the commission found deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.The complaint was allowed in part, with the academy directed to comply with the order within 45 days of receiving it.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: America’s rarest fish is bouncing back: Biologists diving into Nevada’s Devils Hole counted 137 pupfish this fall, nearly double the 69 found a year earlier in the only place the species lives in the wild
articles.summary: A fish that can barely grow beyond an inch is showing signs of a remarkable comeback.
articles.body: A fish that can barely grow beyond an inch is showing signs of a remarkable comeback. Nature has a weird way of making life find a way, even in places where survival seems almost impossible. Sometimes, it is a tiny fish living in a water-filled cavern, far removed from the rest of the world, that reminds us of just how resilient life can be. Deep inside a water-filled cavern in Nevada's Death Valley National Park, one of the world's rarest fish species is slowly rebuilding its population. The Devils Hole pupfish, which exists naturally in only one location on Earth, was once pushed dangerously close to extinction. However, a recent survey has offered conservationists a reason for optimism, with the number of fish recorded in the cavern more than doubling in just one year.According to a news release published by the National Park Service (NPS) on November 3, 2026, biologists counted 137 Devils Hole pupfish during an October 10 survey. This was more than double the 69 fish recorded during the autumn survey in 2025 and nearly twice the 77 observed in spring 2026. The survey was conducted by divers and surface counters from the National Park Service and the US Fish and Wildlife Service, which have monitored the population using these methods since 1972."It's exciting to see Devils Hole pupfish numbers increase so significantly over the past year," said Mike Reynolds, superintendent of Death Valley National Park. "These results reflect the dedication of our scientists and conservation partners working to protect this extraordinary species. While challenges remain, we're encouraged by this progress and committed to its long-term survival."How earthquakes brought the tiny fish close to extinctionThe Devils Hole pupfish (Cyprinodon diabolis) is a small, blue-coloured fish that lives exclusively in Devils Hole, a deep, water-filled limestone cavern in Nevada. Its entire wild population depends on a remarkably small habitat, particularly a shallow limestone shelf measuring approximately 215 square feet, where the fish feed and reproduce.The species has adapted to an environment that would be difficult for many other fish to survive in. The water temperature remains around 90 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit, while oxygen and nutrient levels are relatively low. The pupfish primarily feed on algae growing on the limestone shelf, along with small invertebrates.However, this extremely limited habitat also makes the species vulnerable to even minor environmental disturbances. In December 2024 and February 2025, earthquakes generated powerful waves inside the cavern, disrupting its normally still waters. The waves swept away algae, fish eggs and other organic material from the shallow shelf, affecting both the food supply and breeding grounds of the pupfish.By March 2025, the population had fallen to approximately 20 fish, raising serious concerns about the species' survival. The situation was particularly worrying because the fish has an average lifespan of just 10 to 14 months, leaving little room for prolonged population decline.How conservation efforts helped the population recoverTo prevent the species from disappearing in the wild, conservation teams turned to a captive population maintained at the Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility, located a few miles from Devils Hole. The facility contains a specially designed 100,000-gallon tank that recreates important features of the fish's natural habitat, allowing researchers to maintain a backup population and study its behaviour.Between March 2025 and February 2026, scientists released 72 captive-raised pupfish into Devils Hole. This marked the first time that captive-raised Devils Hole pupfish had been returned to their natural habitat. Conservation teams also provided supplemental food while the algae on the limestone shelf recovered, using research conducted at the facility to guide their efforts.Interestingly, biologists believe that most of the 137 fish recorded during the latest survey were not among those directly released into the cavern. Given the species' short lifespan, researchers believe most of them hatched and grew naturally inside Devils Hole, suggesting that the population has begun reproducing successfully again in its original habitat.The recovery is particularly significant for a species that has faced decades of environmental pressure. The Devils Hole pupfish was listed as endangered in 1967, with groundwater extraction for agriculture and ranching posing a major threat to its habitat. A landmark 1976 US Supreme Court decision, in the case of Cappaert v. United States, upheld protections preventing groundwater pumping from lowering water levels in a way that would threaten the fish's habitat.Although the latest count offers encouraging signs, conservationists caution that the species remains vulnerable to earthquakes, fluctuations in water levels and changes in its food supply. Its entire wild population continues to depend on a single, isolated cavern.For now, the return of the tiny pupfish offers a reminder of what sustained conservation, scientific monitoring and carefully planned intervention can achieve. While 137 fish may seem like a modest number, for a species that had fallen to just 20, every new generation represents another opportunity for survival.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Florida State University student joined a bone marrow registry in 2019; her donation saved a 7-year-old boy's life, and years later, he finally met the woman who gave him a second chance
articles.summary: A decision made during a university recruitment drive in 2019 eventually brought 27-year-old Hope Miller face to face with seven-year-old Samuel Moore,
articles.body: A decision made during a university recruitment drive in 2019 eventually brought 27-year-old Hope Miller face to face with seven-year-old Samuel Moore, whose life she helped save. Miller had joined the Gift of Life Marrow Registry while studying at Florida State University, unaware of who might one day need her help. A few years later, she was identified as a match for Samuel, who had been diagnosed with a rare inherited immune disorder at the age of three. She agreed to donate her bone marrow, giving him an opportunity to undergo a life-saving transplant. The two finally met at a charity gala in Los Angeles on November 16, 2026, turning an anonymous act of generosity into an emotional reunion.A student's 2019 bone marrow registry sign-up led to a life-saving matchMiller joined the Gift of Life Marrow Registry in 2019 during a donor recruitment drive held at Florida State University. By registering, she made herself available to be matched with a patient who needed a bone marrow or blood stem cell transplant.The match eventually came in the form of Samuel, who was just three years old when he was diagnosed with DOCK8 deficiency, a rare inherited immune disorder. The condition affects the body's ability to fight infections and can leave patients vulnerable to severe and potentially life-threatening illnesses.When Miller learnt that she was a match for the young boy, she agreed to donate. She said she made the decision after speaking with her family and considering how she would feel if someone close to her needed such help. Learning that the recipient was a little boy also made the decision particularly personal, as she has brothers.Seven-year-old Samuel was diagnosed with a rare immune disorderDOCK8 deficiency is a genetic condition that affects the immune system, leaving those diagnosed with it at risk of serious and recurring infections. Children with the disorder can experience viral, bacterial and fungal infections, along with other complications.Samuel's diagnosis at the age of three meant that his family had to navigate a difficult medical journey. His mother, Christy Moore, said they were relieved to learn that a bone marrow transplant could save his life.She also spoke about the uncertainty of depending on an unknown person to make the decision to donate. The family was grateful that someone who had never met Samuel was willing to help him.Miller's donation provided the marrow needed for Samuel's transplant, offering him a chance at a healthier future.Donor and recipient meet for the first time at Los Angeles galaThe long-awaited meeting took place during Gift of Life Marrow Registry's One Huge Night gala at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel in Los Angeles on November 16, 2026. Miller and Samuel came face to face for the first time at the event, which brought together donors, transplant recipients, supporters and advocates.Miller said she had hoped that if anyone in her own family ever needed a donation, another person would be willing to step forward. Her decision to join the registry eventually connected her with a child whose life depended on finding a compatible donor.For Samuel's family, the meeting offered an opportunity to thank the woman whose willingness to donate had helped make his treatment possible.Another donor-recipient pair reunites at the eventThe gala also witnessed another emotional reunion between donor Max Mandel and 32-year-old Juan Santoyo of Wasco, California.Mandel, a Los Angeles native now living in New York City, had joined the registry in 2015 while studying in Jerusalem. He later donated blood stem cells to Santoyo, helping save his life after he was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.Santoyo was a husband and father when he became ill, and his wife was pregnant with their second child at the time. His reunion with Mandel brought together two people whose lives had become connected through the donation process.Unlike Miller, who donated bone marrow, Mandel provided peripheral blood stem cells, another method used in transplants.How the Gift of Life Marrow Registry connects donors with patientsGift of Life Marrow Registry is a US-based nonprofit organisation established in 1991. It works to facilitate bone marrow and blood stem cell transplants for patients with conditions including leukaemia, lymphoma and inherited immune disorders.People can register as potential donors through a cheek-swab process that allows their tissue type to be recorded. When a patient needs a transplant, the registry is searched for a compatible match. Further testing is conducted before a donation can proceed.Depending on the patient's medical needs, a donor may provide blood stem cells or bone marrow. Miller and Mandel's stories illustrate how people who have never met can become connected through a decision to register and help someone in need.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Why solutions sometimes make the problem worse? Experts debate at Harvard
articles.summary: On October 18 at Harvard Medical School, about 110 Iranian scientists, engineers, founders and investors spent an hour on a question that sounds simple:
articles.body: On October 18 at Harvard Medical School, about 110 Iranian scientists, engineers, founders and investors spent an hour on a question that sounds simple: why do well-intentioned decisions so often make a problem worse?The discussion was the centerpiece of the third 2See Summit, organized by Mehrzad Sajjadi and Saleh Dadkhahipour, hosts of the Persian-language 2See Podcast. It followed summits at Stanford University in July and the University of Southern California in August. The organizers say more than 300 people attended the three events.As at the earlier summits, Sajjadi and Dadkhahipour opened with a live recording of the podcast instead of a conventional panel. Their guests were Hazhir Rahmandad, the Schussel Family Professor of Management Science and a professor of system dynamics at the MIT Sloan School of Management, and Mohammad Jalali, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School based at the MGH Institute for Technology Assessment. Both work in system dynamics, a field that models how the parts of a complex system feed back on one another over time.The two professors walked through cases from forest fire management, hospital operations, addiction treatment and health policy in which a fix aimed at the visible symptom ended up strengthening the underlying cause. The conversation then moved to artificial intelligence. AI can help decision-makers test a policy before committing to it, the guests argued, but a model handed a poorly framed problem will return a polished answer to the wrong question. They also took up the future of work, Iran's demographic window, the distance between researchers and policymakers, and declining social trust."Most of us are trained to solve the problem in front of us," Sajjadi said. "Systems thinking asks what your solution does to everything around it. That applies to a health policy, a startup or an AI model.""The distance between the people who study a problem and the people who decide on it came up again and again," Dadkhahipour said.After the recording, the summit moved into a networking session. Attendees worked at companies and universities including Microsoft, MIT, Pfizer, Moderna and Fidelity Investments, though none of these organizations was involved in the event. Where the Stanford audience leaned toward AI laboratories and Silicon Valley startups, the Boston room added a large contingent from biotechnology and pharmaceuticals.The second summit was held at USC in Los Angeles on August 22 with more than 100 attendees. That live episode featured Kiana Aran, an associate professor of bioengineering and medicine at UC San Diego and co-founder of the graphene biosensor company Cardea Bio, and Salman Avestimehr, a Dean's Professor at USC and inaugural director of the USC-Amazon Center on Trustworthy AI. They discussed the meeting point of electronics and biology, automated laboratories, AI systems that propose hypotheses and design experiments, and how to tell when university research is ready to become a company.The series began on July 18 at Stanford, where nearly 120 people heard the hosts connect Cold War deterrence theory to the contest between open and closed frontier AI models.Dadkhahipour earned his MBA from Stanford Graduate School of Business and is pursuing a Master in Public Administration at Harvard Kennedy School. Sajjadi is pursuing an MBA and a master's in computer science at Stanford and a master's in biotechnology at Harvard. Before Stanford he was a robotics engineer at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and founded nFlux, an AI computer-vision company focused on manufacturing, which he exited to Invisible AI in 2025.The two started 2See in November 2025 from their dorm rooms at Stanford and Harvard. The show has released 48 episodes and, according to the hosts, has more than 300,000 followers across platforms. The name 2See is pronounced like "Tusi" in Persian, a reference to the 13th-century Iranian polymath Nasir al-Din Tusi. The word also means "grey" in Persian and reads as "to see" in English."In every city we heard the same thing: people knew the names in the room but had never met," Dadkhahipour said. "Silicon Valley, Los Angeles and Boston all have deep Iranian talent. What was missing was a reason to be in the same room."The organizers say a fourth summit is planned for New York. The Harvard conversation with Rahmandad and Jalali was released as episode 46 of the podcast.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Bristol's 600-year-old Ashton Court Mansion could finally be restored after councillors backed a 125-year lease to a community trust, but the group has raised only £125,000 toward its early funding target
articles.summary: Some buildings outlive the generations that built them, quietly carrying fragments of a city's history in their walls, corridors and forgotten rooms.
articles.body: Some buildings outlive the generations that built them, quietly carrying fragments of a city's history in their walls, corridors and forgotten rooms. They witness changing fortunes, shifting ideas of wealth and power, and the transformation of the neighbourhoods around them. But time does not always preserve a building simply because it has stood for centuries. Sometimes, the harder question is whether a city can find a reason, and the resources, to keep its history alive.In Bristol, England, one such building has been waiting for a second life. Ashton Court Mansion, whose oldest surviving parts date back to the 14th century, has seen centuries of change, from its origins as a country estate to its years as a public landmark. Yet much of the historic mansion has remained inaccessible and in poor condition for years, with restoration plans repeatedly struggling to find a sustainable financial future. Now, a community trust hopes to change that, not by turning the building into a private property, but by bringing it back into public and community life.The effort has received an important boost after Bristol City Council councillors backed a proposed 125-year lease of the Grade I-listed mansion to Ashton Court Mansion Trust. However, the road to restoration is far from complete. The trust has raised around £125,000 through its community share offer, against a minimum fundraising target of £480,000 needed to establish its operations and support its early plans.A 125-year lease offers a new possibility for the historic mansionAccording to Bristol City Council's official decision record, the Strategy and Resources Policy Committee approved the proposal on November 16, 2026, endorsing the trust's business plan and authorising the necessary steps towards entering into a long-term lease. The arrangement is intended to allow the trust to regenerate the mansion and provide wider benefits and public access for people in Bristol, North Somerset and visitors.The decision is an important step, but the lease has not yet been formally signed. It is also subject to a call-in period, with the council's decision record stating that it will come into force on November 24 if it is not called in by the November 23 deadline.Under the proposed arrangement, Bristol City Council will retain ownership of the mansion, while the trust will take responsibility for managing, maintaining and restoring the historic building. The long-term lease is expected to give the organisation greater certainty when applying for heritage grants, attracting investment and raising the substantial funds needed for restoration.The trust's plans also involve gradually bringing more of the mansion into use. Rather than attempting to restore the entire property at once, the proposal follows a phased approach, allowing individual rooms and sections to reopen as funding becomes available. The wider Ashton Court Estate, including its parkland, deer park and public facilities, will remain under council management.Why restoring a 600-year-old mansion is proving difficultThe history of Ashton Court Mansion stretches back much further than its current restoration efforts. A manor at Ashton Court was recorded in the Domesday Book, while the oldest surviving core of the present house dates from the late 14th century. The Smyth family acquired the estate in the 1600s and successive generations expanded and remodelled the property over the following centuries.However, maintaining a large historic country house is an expensive undertaking, and the mansion's decline began long before its present restoration plans. According to the trust's account of the building's history, the Smyth estate faced financial difficulties during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with death duties, two world wars and rising maintenance costs putting increasing pressure on the family. By the time Bristol City Council purchased the estate in 1959, the mansion was already in a severely deteriorated condition.Although repair and restoration work was undertaken over the years, unexpected structural problems and competing financial priorities meant that much of the interior remained unfinished. An arson attack in 2013 also caused serious damage to the library in the West Wing. The mansion has remained on Historic England's Heritage at Risk register for more than a decade, while around three-quarters of its interior has been described as derelict or unusable.The scale of the challenge is reflected in the trust's financial estimates. Its business plan anticipates that a full regeneration could require investment of up to £25 million over approximately 20 years. The first five-year phase alone is estimated to cost around £12 million, with major grants, institutional funding, philanthropy and fundraising expected to contribute towards the work.The community fundraising challenge behind the restorationAlongside the proposed lease, Ashton Court Mansion Trust has launched a community share offer to build the financial foundation needed to take on the building. The offer opened on October 21, inviting members of the public to invest in the organisation and become part of its future.The trust has raised approximately £125,000 so far. Its share offer document sets a minimum target of £480,000, an optimum target of £500,000 and a maximum of £550,000. The money is intended to provide working capital for operating the mansion and delivering its charitable activities during the early years. It is important to note that this is not the entire restoration fund; the much larger building programme will require separate grants, donations and investment.Simon Cook, chair of Ashton Court Mansion Trust, said the community share offer had raised £125,000 in its first three weeks, representing 25% of its £500,000 target. He said: "That is a fantastic response, but we still need to raise the remaining £375,000 to provide the working capital needed to operate the building and build the charity that will deliver both community benefit and restoration of the building."The trust's vision extends beyond simply repairing the mansion's walls and roof. Its plans include cultural and artistic activities, heritage programmes, learning opportunities, workspaces, hospitality and community events. Commercial activities, including weddings and private events, are also expected to generate income to support the building's long-term upkeep and charitable work.For now, the council's backing has given the restoration campaign a significant opening, but the difficult work of securing funding and bringing the building back into use remains. A mansion that has stood through centuries of change cannot be restored overnight, and its next chapter will depend on more than a lease or a fundraising campaign. It will require a sustained effort to make the building useful and accessible again, so that Ashton Court is not remembered only as a piece of Bristol's past, but can once again become part of its everyday life.You use AI every day. articles.title: Taiwan flags nearly 2,700 China-linked accounts to Meta over alleged election influence campaign
articles.summary: Taiwan has flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it suspects are part of a Chinese influence campaign aimed at shaping public opinion
articles.body: Taiwan has flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it suspects are part of a Chinese influence campaign aimed at shaping public opinion ahead of local elections next week, according to three Taiwanese government officials and internal reports reviewed by Reuters.The accounts, most of which were created in the past four months, were identified on Threads, Meta's text-based social media platform popular in Taiwan. Officials believe the accounts were created in batches and used to amplify divisive political narratives, discourage voter participation and undermine confidence in democracy.Taiwanese officials also told Meta that around 260 accounts had circulated more than 2,150 AI-generated videos targeting politicians and policies of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), including its Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen. The videos attracted 2.35 million interactions, including comments and shares, according to an internal government report.Meta said it had removed the accounts flagged by Taiwan, many of which had already been disabled by its own systems. The company said none of the accounts had posted about election-related topics and most had no followers.The November 28 elections for mayors and county chiefs are being viewed as an important indicator of support for President Lai Ching-te's DPP ahead of the presidential elections in early 2028. China considers the party a "separatist" force and refuses to engage with it.Accounts allegedly created in batchesAccording to one Taiwanese government report, of the 2,400 Threads accounts flagged by the authorities, 74% listed China as their location, around 25% did not disclose a location and 1% listed Russia.The accounts were divided into 27 clusters, with similar Chinese names and different numerical IDs, suggesting they had been created in batches."The assessment is that this batch of accounts was created in bulk by operators in China or Russia, likely with the aim of influencing Taiwan's 2026 local elections," the report said.Officials said the accounts initially attempted to appear as ordinary Taiwanese users by sharing content about everyday interests, including fortune-telling, to build credibility before turning to political messaging."Then one day, they start by criticising the government and attacking candidates, before saying they are disappointed with the ruling party and will therefore give up voting," one official said.Taiwanese security officials said the suspected campaign was not necessarily aimed at promoting particular candidates but at deepening political divisions and discouraging people from voting."They don't necessarily ask you to support certain candidates but they make people turn against each other, grow disgusted with democracy, choose not to vote, and they intensify election divisions," one of the officials said.The three security officials spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.AI-generated videos target DPP candidateTaiwan also flagged around 260 accounts that officials said had disseminated more than 2,150 AI-generated videos as part of the suspected influence campaign.According to an internal report, the videos received 2.35 million interactions, including comments and shares. Most targeted DPP politicians and policies.Among those targeted was Puma Shen, the party's high-profile candidate for mayor of Taipei. Some videos accused Shen of bullying when he was a student. Shen has denied the allegations.Officials said Threads appeared to be the focus of the suspected operation because of its popularity in Taiwan. They said they had not identified similar accounts on Instagram.Meta says accounts have been removedA Meta spokesperson said the company had removed the accounts flagged by Taiwan's government, adding that many had already been disabled by its systems.None of these "low-quality fake accounts" had posted about election-related topics and most had no followers, the spokesperson said in a statement, adding, "We will continue to take action against accounts that violate our policies."Taiwanese officials said they had confirmed that some of the accounts had been taken down.An official from Taiwan's National Security Council told Reuters that China had used social media platforms and other means to try to influence discourse around the island's elections. Taipei would continue working with allies and responsible platforms to ensure the polls were not affected by foreign forces, the official said.China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to a request for comment. Beijing has long rejected accusations that it interferes in Taiwan's elections.China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, while Taipei rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims.You use AI every day. articles.title: Taiwan lost 25 workers and battled 15 years of flooding and collapses to build the Hsuehshan Tunnel; the payoff was cutting a punishing two-hour mountain drive down to 30 minutes
articles.summary: Explore the remarkable story of the Hsuehshan Tunnel in Taiwan, a 15-year engineering feat marked by challenges, worker sacrifices, and groundbreaking technology that reduced travel time between Taipei and Yilan from two hours to just 30 minutes.
articles.body: For decades, travelling between Taipei and Yilan in northeastern Taiwan meant taking a winding mountain route that could take around two hours. The Hsuehshan Range stood between the capital and the Lanyang Plain, making the journey difficult for residents, commuters and businesses. Taiwan eventually built a highway through the mountains. The result was the Hsuehshan Tunnel, a 12.9 km underground passage that opened on June 16, 2006. It reduced the Taipei-to-Yilan journey to as little as 30 minutes, according to Taiwan’s Executive Yuan.The project took 15 years to complete, according to the Taipei Times and it came at a high cost in both human lives and engineering setbacks. According to a Taipei Times report published shortly after the project opened, 25 workers died during the larger Taipei-Yilan Expressway project and crews faced repeated ground collapses, underground flooding and tunnel boring machines trapped in the rock.Mountain with difficult geological conditionsWork on the project started in 1991. The project involved the creation of two tunnels for roads; one for each direction of traffic flow and an auxiliary pilot tunnel between them. Geologists faced the task of drilling the two main tunnels through the highly fractured bedrock with high water content in the northeastern part of the Hsuehshan Range. To complete the task, engineers resorted to using tunnel boring machines (TBMs). TBMs cut through bedrock and the lined tunnel used pre-fabricated concrete segments. Moreover, the pilot tunnel provided the opportunity to study the conditions underground and gain information for building two road tunnels.A 2005 technical paper on the project’s revised construction plan, presented at an international tunnelling conference, counted 98 major shear and fracture zones along the tunnel. It also recorded 36 cases of groundwater inflow, 42 collapses during drilling and excavation and 13 cases in which the pilot tunnel’s boring machine jammed.Trapped tunnel boring machine forced a change in planOne of the major problems occurred at the westbound main tunnel, where the TBM got stuck close to the Shanghsin Fault. This occurred in September 1997, when the machine encountered very difficult ground conditions and had to be stopped for ground treatment. It started again in December, but the difficulties quickly reappeared. A huge amount of water and soil was pushed into the tunnel on December 14, 1997. The precast concrete support sections in the machine’s rear shield were damaged, and the ground collapsed onto the machine, burying it under debris.The machine could not be recovered for the rest of the construction project. A technical paper by the project’s engineers explained how the collapse and flooding led to the decision. Engineers switched to conventional drill-and-blast excavation for the remaining westbound section. This method involved drilling holes into the rock, placing explosives and removing the broken material before reinforcing the newly excavated surfaces. The change added significant delays to the construction schedule.A 30-minute journey between Taipei and YilanFinally, breakthrough was achieved in the pilot tunnel in October 2003, while the excavation of the main tunnels was completed in September 2004. The Hsuehshan Tunnel was officially commissioned for operation on June 16, 2006, in connection with National Freeway No. 5, or Chiang Wei-shui Freeway. At 12.9 km, it became Taiwan’s longest road tunnel. The Freeway Bureau described it as a twin tunnel with two traffic lanes in each direction. Drivers can pass through the tunnel in about 10 minutes, while the full highway connection reduced the journey between Taipei and Yilan from around two hours to as little as 30 minutes.Travel between the two regions became much easier because the tunnel cuts straight through the Hsuehshan Range instead of sending drivers over a winding mountain road. People who used to find it tough to reach Yilan can now easily access the region from the capital. The completion of the tunnel was the result of years of construction that faced many challenges due to fractures in the rocks, surges in the groundwater levels, collapses and failure of machinery.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1972 thirteen villagers spent five years chiselling a road through a Chinese cliff by hand; the Guoliang Tunnel, its windows cut into the rock face, is now a popular tourist attraction
articles.summary: Discover the Guoliang Tunnel, a breathtaking hand-carved road through a cliff in China's Taihang Mountains, built by 13 villagers in five years. Explore its history, stunning design, and its transformation from a lifeline to a tourist hotspot.
articles.body: A narrow road cuts through a towering red rock cliff in China’s Taihang Mountains. Known as the Guoliang Tunnel, the road connects Guoliang village in Henan Province with the surrounding region. According to Henan Government portal, construction began in 1972, when 13 villagers set out to carve a route through the mountain using basic hand tools. The work took five years. Without heavy construction machinery, the villagers relied on hammers and chisels to break through solid rock. They gradually removed the stone and extended the passage along the cliff. More residents joined the original team as the project progressed. The tunnel was completed in 1977 and measured about 1,250 m.A village with a difficult way outThe village of Guoliang is situated at the top of the Taihang Mountains in Huixian County, Henan Province. Access to the village before the building of the tunnel was through a steep stairway carved out of the mountainside. It was called the “Sky Ladder” and consisted of some 720 steps, according to The Star. According to Xinhua News Agency, the isolation of the village caused serious difficulties in the daily life of its inhabitants. It was especially complicated in cases of medical emergencies when the patient first needed to be taken out of the mountains. In 1972, the decision was made to build a path across the mountain. Thirteen people joined the volunteer work crew for that task. They started their work by hacking the rock with hammers and chisels.Five years of work with hand toolsThe process was time-consuming and physically tiring. Labourers broke down the rock into small portions and removed the waste as the tunnel was formed bit by bit. According to Xinhua’s account of the tunnel’s history, more villagers joined the original group as construction went on. The tunnel is about 5 metres high and 4 metres wide, according to Shanghai Daily. The tunnel has more than 30 openings cut through the rock wall, which Xinhua describes as rock windows. They let in natural light and offer a view of the surroundings from inside. They were also what made the tunnel stand out. Because the road was cut directly into the rock, the openings look out over the valley and the sheer drop beside the narrow road. The tunnel opened to the public in 1977 and gave villagers a shorter route to neighbouring towns. It made it easier to transport goods into Guoliang and agricultural products out of the village.From a lifeline to a tourist attractionIn the end, the tunnel attracted tourists interested in its unique design and beautiful mountain location. Guoliang became famous for its road, which gave locals more chances to make a living. About 1.4 million domestic and foreign tourists visited Guoliang in 2018, according to a 2019 China Daily report.Tourism helped sustain many guesthouses, local restaurants and small shops that gave residents an additional source of income. Guoliang Tunnel is both a transport route and a tourist attraction. They drive through its narrow and rocky passage and are amazed by its history when locals started building it using primitive tools and got help from the community, turning it into a permanent road. Built as a solution to the practical problem of isolation, the passage became a notable feature of Henan Province. The construction of the tunnel was done locally and the labour was provided by locals themselves.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A grandmother lost her four-decade family history manuscript at an airport; a stranger found it and mailed it to her old address, and her family wrapped it up as a Christmas present
articles.summary: Everyone hopes for a Christmas miracle, but for Marsha Hinman, a retired school teacher from Western New York, it came in the form of a stranger's simple
articles.body: Everyone hopes for a Christmas miracle, but for Marsha Hinman, a retired school teacher from Western New York, it came in the form of a stranger's simple act of kindness. Someone she had never met decided that her handwritten family history was too precious to leave behind. After finding the manuscript Hinman had lost at an airport, the stranger mailed it to an old address listed inside. Her family received it and, on Christmas, her children wrapped the long-lost manuscript and gave it to her as a surprise present! "I fell to the floor sobbing," Hinman told ABC News. Now, that's what you call a Christmas miracle!A book that took four decades to completeFor nearly four decades, Marsha Hinman of Spencerport, New York, had been writing down her family's story. Hinman's husband, Dan, had a long battle with multiple sclerosis and died in 1999, just three months before their first grandchild was born. Dan never met any of the children who came after. Wanting them to know who their grandfather was, Hinman began putting their family's memories, struggles and milestones into a book. The project grew into a large, spiral-bound volume.“He never met any of his grandchildren,” Hinman told Rochester. “So I thought, ‘I've got to write something so they know who he was and the legacy he had and how much the Spencerport and Brockport community cared for us.’”Hinman was serious about the book. Her five children eventually had 16 grandchildren between them, and the manuscript kept growing with the family. Each chapter held another piece of a life that had branched out in ways she could not have planned when she started.Then she lost the book at the airportHinman took the book with her on a trip to Florida ahead of Thanksgiving 2019. She planned to finish a few pages at Punta Gorda Airport on the way home, near Fort Myers, where she had a little time to herself before the flight. She didn't really get the chance to finish the book. She boarded the plane, only to realise that the manuscript was not in her bag. It was still at the airport. She told a flight attendant that she had to go back for it. The crew told her she could not leave the plane.“This book is my life. It's my whole life. It's not just a book. It's like my memoirs,” Hinman protested.She contacted the airport, only to realise that the manuscript could have been lost forever. "I did everything I thought I could to get it back," she told WHAM. But it didn't happen, at least not yet. All she could do was pray. “Because I needed a miracle.”The Christmas miracleMiracles don't always happen the way we imagine them. For Marsha Hinman, this one arrived in the most unexpected way. Someone at the airport found the book, looked through its pages for a clue to who owned it and found an old address written inside.That stranger mailed the manuscript, along with a note, to that address in Spencerport. The family who lived there now had no connection to the Hinmans beyond the house. But the homeowner recognised what the package might mean and reached out to Hinman's son about it. He went to pick up the book.Hinman had no idea any of this was happening. She was still waiting for news she wasn't sure would come. And it came wrapped as a Christmas present.When Hinman pulled off the wrapping paper, she was over the moon. Her family, who had watched her search and pray, saw the moment her face changed.“I fell to the floor sobbing. And I'm crying and I couldn't stop. I just can't tell you how much it meant for me to get this book back,” she told the outlet. “It seems so funny to think the book is a Christmas miracle. But it has so much of my life in it.”Hinman had two chapters left to write, and she began work as soon as she received the manuscript. The Christmas miracle was made possible by a kind stranger.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Satellite images show western Nebraska before and after March 2026’s fires; the Morrill Fire burned more than 640,000 acres in a week, becoming one of the state’s largest recorded wildfires
articles.summary: Discover how the Morrill Fire devastated western Nebraska in March 2026, burning more than 640,000 acres in just a week and reshaping the landscape, as seen in NASA's striking satellite imagery.
articles.body: Small problems have a way of turning into something much bigger than anyone expects. A wildfire in western Nebraska did just that in a matter of hours. On the afternoon of 12 March 2026, the fire started in Morrill County. NASA’s Earth Observatory reported that strong winds pushed the fire across the prairie about 110 kilometres (70 miles) in just 12 hours. The Morrill Fire then burned more than 640,000 acres (260,000 hectares) in one week. That made it the biggest wildfire in the state's history.What satellite sawNASA released the before-and-after view image as their Earth Observatory image of the day on 31 March 2026. It was made using two images captured by the VIIRS sensor on board the NOAA-21 satellite. These images show how grasslands of western Nebraska changed before and after multiple fires occurred there. The first image was captured on 28 February 2026, while the second image was taken on 29 March 2026. Both use false colour, which helps to distinguish burned land from unburned land. The grasslands near the North Platte River in the first image are shown in light green and brown colours. In the second image, a large tan patch appears, indicating that the land has been burned. The second image shows how the landscape changed in about one month. By 29 March, authorities reported that the Morrill Fire was fully contained. Crews were still working on two smaller fires to the northeast, called Ashby and Minor, which had started early on 26 March.Why the grass burned so fast The conditions were set long before the first flame was lit. On 20 March 2026, the National Interagency Fire Center issued an advisory for the Northern and Central Great Plains. In March, it said, extreme rates of fire spread were being driven by historically dry fuels. It also pointed to a snow drought that had left the grass dried out and standing upright, which allowed fire to move faster. Since mid-December, the weather had been warmer and windier than usual. Much of the region also received less than half of its normal precipitation over 90 days. The area of concern included western and southern South Dakota, eastern Wyoming and all but southeastern Nebraska.The advisory cautioned that winds above 35 miles per hour could allow fire to spread through grasslands at a speed of more than 3 to 5 miles per hour. Some wildfires in Nebraska had already exceeded 100,000 acres, and the forecast for the remaining days of March offered little hope for widespread moisture. Fire activity was also unusually high across the country in early 2026. NASA's write-up noted that as of 27 March, 15,436 fires had burned 1,510,973 acres nationwide, compared to a 10-year average of 9,195 fires that burned 664,792 acres over the same period. It also highlighted that the Great Plains were highly susceptible to fire in early 2026, with unusual fire behaviour for the time of year.What was lost on the ground News reports cited by NASA indicated that the fires affected large areas of ranch and pastureland. They destroyed homes, barns, fences and injured or killed livestock. The Morrill Fire also burned across much of the Crescent Lake National Wildlife Refuge in the Nebraska Sandhills, an area of grasslands, wetlands and dunes that migratory birds use. Still, there were reports of hundreds of thousands of sandhill cranes making their annual migration through the Platte River valley. Together, the images and the reports show just how quickly a fire can grow when the land is this dry.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Florida biologist Ian Bartoszek uses 40 radio-tagged male pythons as scout snakes to find breeding females, and his team pulled a record 8,080 pounds of invasive Burmese pythons out of Southwest Florida in one season
articles.summary: Florida biologist Ian Bartoszek and his team are using 40 radio-tagged male Burmese pythons as “scout snakes” to locate breeding females, helping remove a
articles.body: Florida biologist Ian Bartoszek and his team are using 40 radio-tagged male Burmese pythons as “scout snakes” to locate breeding females, helping remove a record 8,080 pounds of invasive pythons from Southwest Florida in a single season. The Conservancy of Southwest Florida said its team removed 177 pythons between November 2025 and April 2026, the highest seasonal removal by weight since its programme began in 2013. The tagged males help researchers track down large females before they lay eggs. The team also removed 4,100 python eggs during the season as part of its efforts to suppress the invasive population and protect native wildlife.How 40 radio-tagged male pythons help Florida biologist find breeding femalesAccording to the Conservancy, its science team uses 40 radio-tagged male Burmese pythons to locate breeding snakes during the mating season. Researchers track the males using radio telemetry, following their movements through the landscape to locate female pythons they are mating with. This allows biologists to capture the females before they lay eggs.The programme uses the tagged males as tracking tools rather than relying solely on searching for pythons directly. The Conservancy said the scout snakes helped its team locate large breeding females deep in the landscape during the latest season. The approach is part of its long-term research and removal programme, which has been operating since 2013.Florida team removes record 8,080 pounds of pythonsThe Conservancy of Southwest Florida said its team removed 177 invasive Burmese pythons weighing a combined 8,080 pounds during the November 2025 to April 2026 breeding season. The organisation described this as the greatest biomass of pythons removed in a single season by its tracking team and volunteers since the programme began.The removed female pythons weighed an average of 95 pounds, while the largest female captured during the season weighed 153 pounds and measured 17 feet long. The Conservancy said the females carried an average of 70 eggs, and a quarter of them contained the remains of white-tailed deer.Florida team removes 4,100 Burmese python eggs in record seasonThe team also removed an additional 4,100 Burmese python eggs from the ecosystem during the season. The Conservancy said the removal effort was intended to prevent the eggs from hatching and adding more invasive snakes to the landscape.“This was our first four-ton removal season. Our tagged scout snakes helped us locate large breeding snakes deep in the landscape before they had a chance to lay eggs,” Ian Bartoszek, wildlife biologist and Conservancy Science Project Manager, said. He added that the science-based management efforts were suppressing local python reproduction and that the organisation hoped removal numbers would decline over time with continued pressure.Burmese python population spreads to another Florida countySince 2013, the Conservancy's python research and removal programme has removed 1,750 pythons weighing more than 53,000 pounds from Southwest Florida. The programme has also contributed to 25 collaborative scientific publications examining Burmese python biology and behaviour. Its research involves collaboration with Rookery Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve, the US Geological Survey, the University of Florida and the South Florida Water Management District.Burmese pythons are invasive predators in Florida, and efforts to remove them are aimed at reducing their impact on native wildlife. In a separate October 2026 report, the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) said an established Burmese python population was also present in Charlotte County, where authorities suspect the snakes initially escaped or were released from captivity. Residents are encouraged to report sightings to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) through the IveGot1 app or its invasive species hotline.You use AI every day. articles.title: India's ageing Barak missile shield gets Rs 1,976 crore upgrade: What changes
articles.summary: The defence ministry has signed a Rs 1,976.40 crore contract with Israel Aerospace Industries for the upgradation and obsolescence management of the Barak
articles.body: The defence ministry has signed a Rs 1,976.40 crore contract with Israel Aerospace Industries for the upgradation and obsolescence management of the Barak point defence missile system fitted on Indian warships. Under the deal, IAI will carry out a comprehensive overhaul of the system's hardware and software, which the ministry says will give naval platforms enhanced features and a potent anti-air defence capability.The announcement stresses capability, but obsolescence management is arguably the heart of the contract. The Barak-1 entered service around 2000 and has been deployed for over two decades on Delhi-class destroyers, Shivalik-class and Brahmaputra-class frigates and the aircraft carrier INS Vikramaditya. Many of its electronic components, processors and sensors are now ageing, and in several cases the original manufacturers no longer produce spares, making readiness increasingly expensive to sustain.Two practical considerations explain the need for modernisation of the point defence system. Replacing every installation would cost far more and disrupt operations more than upgrading systems already integrated into the fleet, and many of these ships will serve for years. DRDO's indigenous VL-SRSAM is meant to succeed the Barak-1, but fleet-wide induction will take time. The upgrade ensures no capability gap in the interim. Better software, computing power and fire-control can improve reaction time, reliability, availability and resistance to jamming, even if the missile itself remains the same.The deal also underlines why point-defence systems matter. They form the last layer of an integrated air-defence network, protecting specific assets such as ships, airbases, radars and command centres against threats that slip past outer defences. On a warship, the Barak-1 is that final missile layer against aircraft, drones and anti-ship missiles. Warships are also equipped with gun based close in weapon systems such as the AK-630 which form the final line of defence.Cheap drones, loitering munitions and faster, low-flying missiles shorten reaction time, while the Russia-Ukraine conflict has shown how massed drones can be used against airbases and logistics hubs. Using costly long-range interceptors against inexpensive drones is an unfavourable trade, so shorter-range systems help conserve missiles for graver threats. The danger is saturation, where a defender runs out of interceptors even after intercepting everything.For India, with airbases and forward positions spread along the northern and western borders, layered cover is essential. DRDO's VSHORADS cleared three flight trials on February 27 this year, and the Integrated Air Defence Weapon System, combining QRSAM, VSHORADS and a laser-based weapon, had its maiden trials on August 23, 2025. The Defence Acquisition Council cleared VSHORADS and medium-range missile procurement for the Army on July 3.The Barak contract is thus less a missile purchase than a sustainment effort. It also reinforces the India-Israel defence partnership, which includes the jointly developed Barak-8.

articles.summary: Australian consumers who believed they were paying a one-off A$2 fee to ask questions on JustAnswer were instead signed up for monthly subscriptions
articles.body: Australian consumers who believed they were paying a one-off A$2 fee to ask questions on JustAnswer were instead signed up for monthly subscriptions costing between A$45 to A$75, prompting the Federal Court to order the company to pay A$10 million in penalties. The ruling follows proceedings brought by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), which found that the online question-and-answer service had misled customers about its pricing and its supposed links with Australian government bodies. The court has also ordered refunds for affected consumers and measures to prevent similar conduct.JustAnswer ordered to pay A$10 million over misleading subscription chargesThe Federal Court's decision, announced by the ACCC on 8 July 2026, addresses two separate types of misleading representations made by JustAnswer LLC. The company admitted that it had breached Australian consumer law by misrepresenting the cost of its service and suggesting that it was affiliated with Australian government organisations.According to the ACCC's media release, the company must pay A$10 million in penalties and refund eligible consumers who were misled between November 2022 and August 2025. The court also ordered JustAnswer to publish a corrective notice, establish a consumer law compliance programme and contribute towards the regulator's legal costs.The decision followed an investigation triggered by complaints from customers who said they had not knowingly agreed to ongoing membership payments.How did the A$2 question service lead to monthly chargesJustAnswer operates an online platform that connects people with subject specialists in areas including medicine, law, accounting and technology. Consumers can access the service through its website, where a chat feature directs them towards asking questions and receiving assistance.The ACCC's September 2025 concise statement, filed in the Federal Court, outlined how the pricing representations were presented to Australian consumers. People searching online for information could encounter JustAnswer through search results or sponsored advertisements before being directed to its website.The chat widget then promoted access for a one-off A$2 joining fee. According to the ACCC, the website used statements indicating that consumers could join for only A$2, with the fee described as fully refundable.However, the payment process also enrolled customers in a recurring subscription. The monthly charges ranged from A$45 to A$75, and customers could be charged even when they did not use the service.JustAnswer admitted that its presentation had represented the A$2 fee as the total cost of accessing the service, despite the additional monthly payments. The ACCC said consumers had not been adequately informed about those ongoing charges before joining.Why were customers charged more than they expectedThe difference between the advertised joining fee and the actual subscription cost was central to the case.The ACCC's September 2025 proceedings initially alleged that customers were being signed up for subscriptions costing around A$50 to A$90 a month. The regulator said the monthly fee was displayed in a way that many consumers might not notice, while the substantially higher ongoing cost was not mentioned until customers reached the payment screen.The final outcome, reported by the ACCC confirmed that the subscription charges involved in the admitted conduct ranged from A$45 to A$75 per month.Customers could face repeated payments after believing they had made a single, relatively small purchase. The charges continued until consumers took action to cancel their subscriptions.ACCC Commissioner Luke Woodward said the unexpected fees had caused financial harm and prevented consumers from making informed decisions. He added that people who had known the full cost might have decided not to use the service.JustAnswer also mislead customers about government affiliationsThe pricing issue was not the only concern addressed by the court. The ACCC's statement also detailed allegations that JustAnswer had presented its services as connected to Australian government agencies or official bodies.The company admitted that between June 2022 and February 2024, it made misleading representations about its affiliation with the Fair Work Ombudsman.The ACCC explained that statements on the website suggested consumers could speak directly with a Fair Work Ombudsman representative. The regulator said those claims implied that JustAnswer was part of, approved by or affiliated with the government agency, when no such relationship existed.The company also admitted making similar misleading representations about an Australian Ombudsman between June 2022 and March 2025.According to the ACCC, some consumers may have used the service believing they were receiving assistance from an independent Australian Ombudsman rather than a private online platform.What must JustAnswer do for affected Australian consumersThe Federal Court's orders extend beyond the financial penalty. The ACCC's July 2026 announcement said JustAnswer must refund Australian consumers who were misled about the A$2 fee and subsequently signed up for the more expensive subscription between November 2022 and August 2025.The company will contact affected customers who complained to JustAnswer or the ACCC and have not already received a full refund.Consumers who were unaware of the monthly membership charges and have not previously complained can also contact JustAnswer to apply for a refund. An injunction prevents it from engaging in similar misleading conduct in the future.JustAnswer admitted that it had breached Australian consumer law and agreed to make joint submissions with the ACCC concerning penalties and other orders. The ACCC's September 2025 proceedings identified subscription traps and misleading online design as broader consumer concerns.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Rubbing salt into Pahalgam victims' wounds': Row over Pakistan minister at SCO meet in Delhi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A political row broke out after Pakistan minister Masood Malik arrived in Delhi on Friday to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO)
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A political row broke out after Pakistan minister Masood Malik arrived in Delhi on Friday to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisation Dialogue. Congress questioned the invitation and accused the BJP-led Centre of “rubbing salt into the wounds of Pahalgam victims’ families”."You keep changing your stance. Sometimes you travel there, sometimes you reach Lahore, at other times you abruptly call off Operation Sindoor, and now you invite them here. What exactly is Prime Minister Modi doing? The funeral pyres of those martyred in the Pahalgam massacre have not even cooled yet, and you are rubbing salt into the wounds of their families,” said Congress spokesperson Supriya Shrinate."The Government of India, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is organising the SCO Civilisational Dialogue in India on November 21 and 22. The question is: why was Pakistan invited to this event? Why have you invited Pakistan, a country that sponsors terrorism in India? You invited Pakistan, and its minister, Musadik Malik, has arrived here," she said.Questioning the "red carpet" treatment being extended to the minister, Shrinate said, "This is the same person who had openly threatened just a few months ago to chop off the hands of Indians and shed our blood.""The question is that Pakistan has not stopped sponsoring terrorism, while Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government is busy welcoming its representatives. Musadik Malik be served biryani, kebabs and kheer? The government is rolling out the red carpet to welcome him. Why does your work not get done without an anti-India Pakistan? The point is that you should also say and do what Rahul Gandhi has stated unequivocally: as long as Pakistan continues to sponsor terrorism, no dialogue with it is possible," she added.J&K Congress President Tariq Hameed Karra also accused the BJP of having "double standards" regarding militancy, Indo-Pakistan talks, or international treaties."Look, as far as the Government of India is concerned, particularly the BJP, they have always had double standards. Whether it is regarding militancy, Indo-Pakistan talks, or international treaties, their approach has consistently been marked by double standards. The very person who made the loudest protests when the Indus Waters Treaty was suspended here had raised more objections than anyone else at that time. But the fact that they are displaying double standards is nothing new," he said."This is another example of their double standards. When our Prime Minister went to Pakistan uninvited, what could be a bigger example of double standards than that? Basically, the BJP has lost its track. Its foreign policy is being handled on a day-to-day basis. It has no consistent or permanent policy towards its neighbouring countries, whether Pakistan, China, Bangladesh or Sri Lanka. They deal with each country according to what suits them at a particular time," he added.Pakistan's federal minister for climate change and environmental coordination Masood Malik arrived in New Delhi to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisation Dialogue. He was received by Pakistan high commissioner's Chargé d'Affaires in India, Saad Warraich. Malik's visit marks the first time a Pakistani minister has travelled to India in three years.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
