articles.title: Hyderabad man pays in advance for two plots in residential township but gets no registrations; Telangana consumer commission orders Rs 5 lakh with 9% interest
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Telangana has directed a developer and its chairman to refund Rs 5 lakh to a man after the company failed to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Telangana has directed a developer and its chairman to refund Rs 5 lakh to a man after the company failed to register two residential plots despite collecting advance payments. The commission held that the developer was guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.What was the dispute about?The complainant, Sanisetty Jagadeesh Babu, a 47-year-old private employee from Hyderabad, entered into two agreements of sale with Pudami Developers for residential plots measuring 200 square yards each in its Sunray City Township Phase-I project at Kadthal, Ranga Reddy district.The first agreement, dated April 8, 2021, was for plot No.253 at Rs 8.4 lakh, while the second, dated August 7, 2021, was for plot No.53 at Rs 8.6 lakh. He paid a total advance of Rs 5 lakh for the two plots, with the remaining amount payable at the time of registration.He alleged that despite expressing his willingness to pay the balance amount, the developers neither accepted it nor initiated steps to register the plots in his name.He further alleged that the company's managing director had shifted business addresses and invested money collected from purchasers in another property at Kolanupaka in Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district.When he traced the developers and demanded registration, they allegedly executed a promissory note on January 29, 2023, promising to repay Rs 5.92 lakh if the plots were not registered.After his legal notice dated October 12, 2023, was returned, he approached the commission seeking registration of the plots or alternative plots, Rs 2 lakh compensation and Rs 50,000 towards litigation costs.The developers did not appear or file their written response despite notices, including newspaper publication. They were proceeded against ex-parte.What did the commission say?The bench comprising president Chitneni Latha Kumari and members D Madhavi Latha and Kathyayani Khandavilli found that the sale agreements and payment receipts established that the developers had collected Rs 5 lakh and agreed to execute registered sale deeds.It also noted that the promissory note for Rs 5.92 lakh supported the complainant's case."The above documentary evidence makes it amply clear that the Opposite Party No.1-Sri Nidamanuri Mohan Rao, Chairman and Managing Director committed deficiency in service and adopted an unfair trade practice," the commission noted.It held that the managing director was liable to refund the amount with interest instead of directing registration of the plots. However, it dismissed the claims against opposite parties 2 to 4.Final orderIn its November 12, 2026 order, the commission partly allowed the complaint and directed opposite party No.1, Nidamanuri Mohan Rao Gupta, to pay:Rs 5 lakh with 9 percent annual interest from August 7, 2021, till realisation.Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.The remaining claims were disallowed. The order must be complied with within 45 days of receipt, failing which the interest rate will increase to 12 percent per annum from the date of default till realisation.

articles.title: Bengaluru man kills 18-year-old stepson, attacks wife with knife and hammer over 'affair'
articles.summary: BENGALURU: A 44-year-old man allegedly attacked his wife and her 18-year-old son with a knife and hammer, killing the teenager and leaving the woman
articles.body: BENGALURU: A 44-year-old man allegedly attacked his wife and her 18-year-old son with a knife and hammer, killing the teenager and leaving the woman injured before locking her inside a room and fleeing following a domestic quarrel in Bengaluru, police said on Friday.The accused was arrested after the incident came to light nearly three days later.The accused, identified as Sudeep, who had previously worked in the private banking sector, allegedly attacked Seema (43) and her son Soham at their apartment in Padmanabhanagar, under Banashankari police station limits, on November 16, police said.Citing preliminary investigation, a senior police officer said Sudeep was Seema's second husband, while Soham was her son from her first marriage.The accused allegedly suspected Seema of having an illicit relationship, triggering a quarrel between them. Seema worked at an insurance company.According to police, the attack took place between 9 pm and 11 pm on November 16, after which Sudeep allegedly fled.The incident came to light following a complaint by B Mallayya, who had rented out his flat in Padmanabhanagar to Seema from October 3, 2024. She was living there with her husband and son.In his complaint, Mallayya said he had received complaints from neighbours over the past six months about frequent quarrels and arguments among the family members.He said he had repeatedly advised them to maintain peace and had also asked them to vacate the flat.On November 16, around 9 pm, the flat owner received calls from neighbours but was at work. About an hour later, he contacted the security guard, who told him there was no disturbance at the flat at that time, the senior police officer said.On the night of November 19, when Mallayya visited the flat, nobody responded from inside. He then went to Banashankari police station along with his friends and alerted the police.Subsequently, Mallayya, police personnel and Seema's friends went to the flat and found it locked. A locksmith was called to open the doors around 11 pm.On entering, they noticed bloodstains on the floor and walls. They then heard Seema screaming from a locked room inside the house, which was opened with the locksmith's help, the officer said.During questioning, Seema told police that Sudeep had quarrelled with her and Soham between 9 pm and 11 pm on November 16 before attacking them.Soham died in the assault, while Sudeep allegedly attempted to kill her as well. Seema sustained injuries but managed to lock herself inside a room.Police found Soham's body in the bathroom.Based on Seema's complaint, police registered a case against Sudeep under sections 103(1) (murder) and 109(1) (attempt to murder) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. He was subsequently arrested, police added.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: UK acts to secure thousands of commercial fridges after Europe cyberattacks
articles.summary: Britain has carried out a major cybersecurity operation to protect tens of thousands of commercial fridges and freezers from potential hacking.
articles.body: Britain has carried out a major cybersecurity operation to protect tens of thousands of commercial fridges and freezers from potential hacking. Recent attacks on refrigeration systems across Europe spoiled food worth millions of euros and disrupted supermarkets.The operation involved major supermarket chains, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, with thousands of devices used to control refrigeration systems taken offline as a precaution. In some cases, staff were asked to physically disconnect internet cables and monitor temperatures manually, the BBC reported.The vulnerability was discovered in late October by ethical hackers at British firm Omega Systems, who examined the security of refrigeration controllers made by Resource Data Management (RDM). Experts at Pen Test Partners helped verify the weakness and alert authorities.The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency joined the effort to warn businesses and plug the security gaps. IT teams at major supermarket chains were diverted to the task, with one employee telling the BBC that hundreds of devices were taken offline each day over a week.The urgency followed a series of attacks on commercial refrigeration systems in Europe. In France, hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites were hit in October after hackers targeted temperature-control systems made by Danish firm Danfoss. A further wave in early November affected stores across seven European countries, with Belgium and Luxembourg among the worst hit.French intelligence and cybersecurity agencies blamed Iran's Revolutionary Guards for the October attack, which reportedly affected around 700 commercial sites and triggered 15 fires after hackers raised temperatures in refrigeration systems. Tehran has denied the accusation.Security researchers warned that Britain's refrigeration controllers had weaknesses, including problems involving weak passwords. However, RDM disputed comparisons with the European attacks, saying exploiting its systems would have required physical access to specific hardware.RDM chief executive Ged Evans said the vulnerability was identified in a test environment and that the assessment involved dismantling the company's hardware. He said the company had already released initial software patches, contacted customers and recommended steps to reduce risks. RDM also said it had found no evidence of malicious activity on its controllers.The BBC said the operation had been kept under wraps to avoid alerting potential attackers before businesses could secure their systems.You use AI every day. articles.title: A federal judge rules Brooke Rollins' religious emails to roughly 100,000 USDA employees unconstitutional and restricts the use of her official account
articles.summary: A US federal judge has ordered Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to stop sending religious messages to employees through her official government email
articles.body: A US federal judge has ordered Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to stop sending religious messages to employees through her official government email account, ruling that her communications crossed boundaries by assuming that staff members shared her Christian beliefs.US District Judge Trina Thompson issued the order on Thursday while granting a preliminary injunction sought by federal employees who accused Rollins of using her position to promote Christianity within the Department of Agriculture (USDA). The judge said the secretary must recognise limits when communicating religious messages and cannot use her official authority to pressure subordinates."The Court ORDERS that the Secretary must recognise certain boundaries when communicating religious messages," Thompson wrote in her ruling.The case was brought by seven USDA employees from different religious backgrounds, including those who do not identify with any religion. They alleged that Rollins had sent increasingly religious messages to the department's entire workforce, making employees feel excluded and pressured to conform to her beliefs.Judge says Rollins crossed boundaries with Christian messagesAccording to the complaint, Rollins began sending department-wide holiday emails shortly after taking office. Some of the messages included references to Jesus Christ, Christmas and the resurrection of Jesus.In a Christmas message sent on December 23, 2025, Rollins said that the spirit of generosity came from "the very first Christmas when God gave us the greatest gift possible, the gift of his Son and our Savior Jesus Christ".In another message sent on Easter, April 5, 2026, she described the occasion as "the greatest story ever told" and referred to employees as being like the first disciples who encountered the risen Christ.The employees argued that the messages amounted to government-sponsored religious promotion and violated the First Amendment's protections against the establishment of religion.Thompson agreed that the communications went too far, finding that they created pressure on employees to accept or appear to share the secretary's religious beliefs.The judge also took issue with Rollins' repeated use of words such as "we", "us" and "our" in the messages, saying the language suggested that employees universally shared her Christian beliefs. She noted that the emails did not acknowledge employees who followed other religions or held no religious beliefs.The court also rejected the argument that employees could simply ignore the messages, pointing out that Rollins used the same official email account to communicate important departmental information, including agency restructuring and government shutdown plans."Why should the secretary be exempt from her own rules? The buck stops with Secretary Rollins," Thompson wrote, adding that her senior position warranted greater scrutiny because she sat at the top of the agency's hierarchy.The judge clarified that the order did not prevent Rollins from expressing her faith in her personal capacity or discussing religion with colleagues who were interested.USDA considers appeal as religious messaging sparks debateThe USDA said it was evaluating all available options, including filing an appeal, and described the ruling as a "completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary".The department had argued that Rollins was merely sharing her personal views about religious holidays and was neither conducting religious exercises nor forcing employees to follow her beliefs.However, Thompson pointed to the department's own November 2025 guidance on religious expression in the workplace, saying Rollins should follow the boundaries outlined in her own directives. The guidance allows employees to discuss their faith with interested colleagues but prohibits persistent unwanted religious advances and the use of official authority to pressure subordinates.The ruling comes amid a wider debate over the role of religion in the Trump administration. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has incorporated Christian prayer into activities at the Pentagon, while critics have accused administration officials of blurring the separation between religion and government.Advocates of church-state separation have also raised concerns over religious messaging by senior officials and the use of government platforms to promote Christianity.The USDA ruling, however, does not prevent Rollins from practising or expressing her faith privately. It restricts the use of her official government communication channels in ways that could amount to religious coercion in the workplace.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: PM Modi speaks to Yogi Adityanath, offers condolences over mother's death
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday spoke to Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath and expressed condolences over the death of his
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday spoke to Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath and expressed condolences over the death of his mother, Savitri Devi, who passed away at the age of 91 in her native village in Uttarakhand's Pauri Garhwal district.Savitri Devi died around 10.45 am on Friday in Panchur village, residents told PTI. She had been unwell for a long time and could recognise only family members, a member of the Panchur Gram Sabha said.Pauri Garhwal Senior Superintendent of Police Sarvesh Panwar said the local administration was in touch with the family.Adityanath was attending a public function in Uttar Pradesh when he received the news of his mother's death. He had two more official engagements scheduled for later in the day and was expected to continue with his programme. It was not immediately clear whether he would travel to Uttarakhand for the last rites, which are likely to be held on Saturday.G C Badola, a member of the Panchur Gram Sabha, told PTI, “One of her sons is posted in Kotdwar and will reach the village by Friday evening. The last rites will likely be conducted at Phool Chatti Ghat near the village on Saturday, where the last rites of Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s father were also held.”Defence minister Rajnath Singh expressed grief over Savitri Devi's death in a post on X, saying the loss of a mother was one of the most unbearable blows in life. He extended his condolences to Adityanath and his family.Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami also described her death as extremely sad and heartbreaking, saying, "Her demise is an irreparable loss to the family." He extended his condolences to the bereaved family and prayed for strength for them to cope with the loss.Uttar Pradesh Deputy Chief Ministers Keshav Prasad Maurya and Brajesh Pathak, along with state BJP president Pankaj Chaudhary, also condoled her death and prayed for peace for the departed soul and strength for the family.Adityanath's father, Anand Singh Bisht, died following a prolonged illness in 2020. His last rites were performed in Uttarakhand. Adityanath did not attend the funeral due to the Covid-19 lockdown and his responsibilities as Uttar Pradesh chief minister.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A Facebook request brought a boy with leukaemia 2,000 patches from across the US; his family later created a project that sends free patch-covered jackets and tote bags to children with cancer
articles.summary: When Oliver Burkhardt was diagnosed with leukaemia, his father, Brian, wanted to find a way to bring some happiness into his life during chemotherapy.
articles.body: When Oliver Burkhardt was diagnosed with leukaemia, his father, Brian, wanted to find a way to bring some happiness into his life during chemotherapy. He turned to Facebook, asking friends to send decorative patches that Oliver could collect and sew onto a jacket.What began as a small request soon reached people beyond the family’s circle. Within a month, Oliver had received 2,000 patches, about 70% of them from strangers. The gesture gave Oliver something to look forward to during treatment. According to The Associated Press, the experience inspired the family to establish the ‘Oliver Patch Project’, which sends free patch-decorated jackets or tote bags to children with cancer across the United States.How Oliver received 2,000 patches during cancer treatmentOliver’s father first thought of the idea in 2020, shortly after his son was diagnosed. Brian noticed some patches lying in a desk drawer and thought receiving similar ones in the mail might cheer Oliver up.Friends could send them even during COVID-19 lockdowns,Brian said, “It’s an easy ask. They can drop a patch in an envelope and, in return, it gave Oliver something to look forward to. Checking the mail every day would get him off the sofa.”Brian shared his request on Facebook, and friends began passing it on to others. The first patch to arrive was a kangaroo. Soon, more patches followed, turning a small request into a much bigger response. Around 2,000 patches arrived that month, with 70% coming from strangers.Oliver surprisingly said, “I was like, ‘Wow, this is all for me?’ I was like genuinely super surprised. They were all different colors and they all had nice notes, like ‘Hope you feel better.’”As he continued treatment, his parents began sewing the patches onto jackets while sitting with him in his hospital room.The patches helped Oliver feel supported during treatmentOliver wore his denim jacket to hospital, with around 50 patches chosen from the thousands that had arrived. They included designs linked to Pokémon, Superman, NASA, police, fire and military services, as well as classic rock bands.The jacket became a source of comfort during treatment and helped start conversations with nurses. His parents also decorated their own jackets, showing that they were a team.Oliver said, “I knew people were looking out for me, they gave me positive vibes, that people loved me.”Seeing the effect on their son, Oliver and his parents decided that other children going through cancer treatment might also appreciate a jacket of their own.‘Oliver Patch Project’ has reached children across all 50 statesThe family launched the ‘Oliver Patch Project’ after reaching out to designer friends, who sent 300 possible patch designs within a day.As of 2024, three years after its launch, the charity had provided more than 1,600 children, from infancy to 19 years old, with a free denim jacket or tote bag. Each child or their parents selected 20 patches from the programme’s website.The charity then sent another patch by mail every month. As of 2024, children with cancer from all 50 states had joined the nationwide programme, and about 30 children enrolled each week. The project was limited to the United States, although funding had also been secured to send patches to sick children taking part in experimental drug trials in the US and 18 other countries.Gorilla, bald eagle and polar bear patches marked different treatment stagesThe project also sent families a box of 13 milestone patches to give children during common cancer treatments or when they experienced side effects.Designs included a gorilla for starting chemotherapy, a bald eagle for hair loss and a polar bear for fever. A child could work towards receiving an ‘I Rang the Bell’ patch after completing a round of treatment.Siblings received special patches too, after Oliver’s parents recognised that his younger brother, Peter, also needed attention during the family’s difficult period. The charity was supported by donors and foundations, while clothing company Perry Ellis donated jackets and tote bags.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Vermont landowner bought land to protect her privacy, but neighbours who used it for decades as a driveway, garden, and recreation space won ownership in a Supreme Court ruling
articles.summary: A Vermont homeowner bought vacant lots between her lakeside property and her neighbours’ land in 1988, intending to create a privacy buffer.
articles.body: A Vermont homeowner bought vacant lots between her lakeside property and her neighbours’ land in 1988, intending to create a privacy buffer. However, the neighbours and their predecessor had already been using parts of the disputed area for years. Their activities included extending a driveway and turnaround, parking vehicles, maintaining a garden and rock steps, and using the land for outdoor recreation.The homeowner later challenged their claim to the strip, which measured about one-tenth of an acre. According to the Vermont Supreme Court's February Term, 2026 ruling in Deborah Tarrant v. Christopher Bartels and Amelia Bartels, the court upheld the ruling granting the neighbours ownership of the disputed land. In 2023, a survey confirmed that the disputed strip was part of her property.How did a privacy buffer become the centre of a property disputeThe homeowner acquired her lakeshore property in 1968. Her neighbours’ predecessor, Mr Gennari, bought the property to the south in 1979. In 1988, she purchased the vacant lots between the two properties to create a privacy buffer. The land lay between a road to the east and Lake Champlain to the west.Mr Gennari later sold his property to his daughter and son-in-law in 2019. The disputed strip measured about one-tenth of an acre and was marked by iron pipes along its northern side.Mr Gennari found the pipes when he bought his property and believed they marked its northern boundary.What did a 2023 survey reveal about the disputed propertyThe neighbours’ driveway and turnaround extended into the disputed strip. They also parked cars and a recreational vehicle there, held parties and played outdoor games. Their other activities included reseeding the lawn several times, maintaining rock stairs and a garden, and using part of the area for a greywater field. The neighbours and their predecessor had used the land continuously from at least the early 1980s.The homeowner did not know until 2003 that the driveway extended onto land for which she held the legal title. In 2023, the plaintiff commissioned a survey that identified the strip as part of her property. The survey prompted the ownership dispute.Driveway, garden and outdoor activities strengthen neighbours' ownership claimThe case began in the Chittenden Unit's civil division. The homeowner filed a lawsuit in September 2023, seeking a declaration that she owned the disputed land and damages for the removal of trees. The neighbours argued that their predecessor had acquired ownership through adverse possession.Under Vermont law, “To achieve title through adverse possession, a claimant must demonstrate that possession of the land was open, notorious, hostile and continuous throughout the statutory period of fifteen years.”The court considered the driveway, turnaround, tree cutting, greywater field, rock stairs, and garden as evidence that the land was used openly, as an owner would. The court also found that permission granted in 2003 did not affect the claim because the 15-year period had already passed.Supreme Court upholds neighbours' ownership through constructive possessionThe homeowner appealed, arguing that the neighbours’ use was not sufficiently visible or extensive and that factual disputes remained. The Supreme Court rejected those arguments, explaining that the test was whether the activities would put a reasonably prudent person on notice, not whether the homeowner could see them from her house or the road.The Vermont Supreme Court ruled in favour of the neighbours, Christopher and Amelia Bartels. It upheld the finding that they had acquired ownership through constructive possession. Under this doctrine, a claimant can gain possession of an entire plot by occupying part of it in qualifying circumstances. The trial court relied on both clear boundaries and colour of title. The Supreme Court affirmed the colour of title, saying that the ground applied even if the clarity of the boundary markers was disputed.It also found that the neighbours' predecessor, Mr Gennari, had acted under colour of title, meaning he believed the iron pipes marked the boundary of his property. The Supreme Court therefore upheld the ruling granting the neighbours ownership of the entire disputed strip.Disclaimer: This article is based on the Vermont Supreme Court's ruling in Deborah Tarrant v. Christopher Bartels and Amelia Bartels. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the property dispute or the claims made by either party.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Your own confession': Rahul, Kharge hit out at PM Modi's 'hunger' jibe at India Inc
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his remarks criticising India Inc for failing to create enough
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his remarks criticising India Inc for failing to create enough jobs and raise employee salaries despite government concessions.Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge accused PM Modi of shifting the blame for his government's economic failures onto industrialists. They alleged that the government's policies had weakened small businesses, encouraged monopolies and failed to generate employment.Responding to PM Modi's remarks at the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) annual convention in New Delhi on Thursday, Rahul Gandhi said the Prime Minister's criticism of industrialists was an admission of his own government's failures."Modi ji, these aren't accusations against them, they're your own confession," Rahul wrote in a post on X.Turning the Prime Minister's remark about India Inc's appetite for government concessions against him, Rahul said the country knew who was really responsible for the situation."You say, 'They're so hungry they can't even fill their stomachs.' Well said. The whole country knows whose hunger this is," he said.Rahul alleged that the government had handed over key sectors, including airports, ports, mines, forests, electricity, coal and roads, to a select group of business interests. He questioned how many jobs these companies had created in return."Airports, ports, mines, forests, electricity, coal, roads, all handed over to them. How many jobs did they create?" he said.The Congress leader also accused the government of damaging small traders and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) through demonetisation and what he called a flawed Goods and Services Tax (GST). He alleged that companies competing fairly had also lost out because of the government's policies."Monopoly doesn't create jobs. It drives up prices and eliminates competition," Rahul said.Taking a swipe at PM Modi's remark that industry leaders expected the government to act while they waited to see the results, Rahul accused the Prime Minister and his associates of benefiting from the system."'You do it, we'll see'? Modi ji, you and your friends did the looting, the country saw it, and is still seeing it," he said.Rahul also took a dig at the lack of applause during the Prime Minister's address. He said the government's policies had left industrialists, small traders, the poor, the middle class and unemployed young people with little reason to cheer."Get your applause and your thali-banging from whatever followers you have left," he said.Kharge accuses PM Modi of blaming industry for his failuresKharge also criticised the Prime Minister, accusing him of holding the business community responsible for economic problems created by his government."But, true to habit, PM Modi blamed the business community for his own failures in his speech at FICCI!" Kharge said."It felt as though the Prime Minister were the leader of the opposition. He has woken up after 12 years," he added.The Congress president defended his party's economic record, saying it had played a key role in opening up the Indian economy."The Congress Party is the mother of economic liberalisation," he said, adding that the country's highest decadal average growth had been recorded during the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government's tenure.Kharge alleged that the Modi government had handed over the country's resources to "1-2 capitalist cronies" while weakening MSMEs and small traders. He said the lack of healthy competition had stifled innovation, affected manufacturing quality and damaged the global reputation of Indian products."Today, there are no jobs, no savings, and inflation is at its peak. PSUs have been shut down, and Make in India has been turned into Buy From China," he said.He further alleged that the BJP had allowed a select group of capitalists to gain structural control of the Indian economy, calling it one of the biggest challenges facing the country.What PM Modi said at FICCIThe Congress leaders' remarks came a day after PM Modi questioned whether Indian companies were doing enough to increase employment and raise salaries despite several concessions from the government.Addressing FICCI's annual general meeting and convention in New Delhi on Thursday, the Prime Minister listed measures taken to improve the business environment. These included reducing the basic corporate tax rate from 30 per cent in 2014 to 22 per cent, simplifying tax returns and refunds, and lowering GST rates on several products.He also referred to income-tax relief for individuals earning up to Rs 12 lakh annually, saying it had increased people's purchasing power.Questioning industry leaders on whether they had passed on the benefits through higher salaries and more jobs, PM Modi said, "I know you won't applaud. I know that very well, because your appetite is so enormous that no matter how much you are given, it is never enough (aapki bhookh itni hai, kitna hi khilao pet bharta hi nahi)."He added, "I have given income tax relief up to Rs 12 lakh. But have you increased the salaries of your employees? Have you increased the number of employees? No! It is always: 'Modi ji, you do it; we will see what happens.' This is how things will continue."The Prime Minister urged industry leaders to take greater responsibility for employee welfare and economic growth instead of relying on the government to do so.PM Modi invokes Gandhi's Swadeshi messagePM Modi also invoked Mahatma Gandhi's call for Swadeshi and self-reliance, questioning why Indian industry still needed to be reminded of the importance of promoting indigenous products.Referring to Gandhi's message from 1930, he said, "Imagine, 100 years have passed, but in 1930, Gandhi left us with this message, and today, so many years later, I too have to say the same thing. Is this your success or your failure? Don't listen to me; at least you could have to listen to Gandhi! (Meri mat mano, par Gandhi kih toh mano bhai). He too spoke of Swadeshi before leaving; he too spoke of Atmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India). And now you have turned 100 years old, yet things remain right where they were ... Spread my message too to every home!"The Prime Minister also recalled an interaction with Income Tax Department officials in Gujarat around 2001-02, when he was chief minister. He said he had urged officials to stop treating taxpayers as potential wrongdoers and instead recognise their contribution to the country."When will you stop treating everyone as a thief? What kind of approach is this? You, too, work for the country. Are we the only ones who have taken it upon ourselves to serve the nation? You also do your bit, and every citizen does their bit. Everyone deserves respect," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: California father stunned as woman claims to be his daughter who vanished at 3 from campground in 1984
articles.summary: A California father was left stunned after a woman turned up at his home claiming to be his daughter, who disappeared from a campground more than four
articles.body: A California father was left stunned after a woman turned up at his home claiming to be his daughter, who disappeared from a campground more than four decades ago. The woman, Cindy Rae Enders, has repeatedly approached the family, identifying 83-year-old Mike Bradbury as her father and his late wife Patty as her mother. However, she has refused to take a DNA test requested by the family to establish whether her claims are genuine.According to a report by the New York Post, Enders has even tattooed the name Laura Ann Bradbury, along with her 1981 birth year, on her leg. She has also started answering to the name Laura and sent letters containing references to family memories and photographs of Patty.Enders has appeared several times outside the Bradbury family's home in Twentynine Palms, San Bernardino County. Her car reportedly carries a personalised number plate bearing the initials LANNB, referring to Laura Ann Bradbury.Despite her claims, questions remain over her identity, particularly because she has repeatedly declined the family's request for an ancestry DNA test.Woman claims memories match missing girl's disappearanceEnders has said that some of her childhood memories match details surrounding Laura's disappearance in October 1984. She recalled walking towards a blue van after a man told her he was Santa Claus. She also claimed that the people who raised her under another name repeatedly suggested that she was not their biological daughter.According to the Los Angeles Times, Enders said she discovered Laura's photographs while researching missing children and recognised similarities between herself and the missing girl.She has also claimed that a man she believed was her biological father told her on his deathbed that she was not his daughter and encouraged her to investigate someone named Mike.However, several details have raised questions about her account. Her birth certificate identifies her as Cindy Rae Enders, born in Loma Linda in 1982, a year after Laura's reported birth in 1981.Her stepfather, James Hunt, has also disputed her claims, alleging that she has a history of making up elaborate stories. Enders has rejected his allegations and maintained that she is attempting to reunite with the family she believes she lost.She reportedly hired private investigator Tony Campbell to examine her claims, but he became doubtful after she resisted DNA testing. Enders has said she would agree to a test conducted by a laboratory whose results could be used in court, rather than the ancestry test requested by the Bradbury family.How did Laura Bradbury disappear?Laura disappeared on October 18, 1984, during a family camping trip to what was then Joshua Tree National Monument in California.Mike was setting up the family's tent when his eight-year-old son, Travis, headed towards a portable restroom, with Laura following him. When Travis returned, his younger sister was nowhere to be found.Her disappearance triggered a massive search operation involving helicopters, bloodhounds and horseback teams, but rescuers could not locate her. The family remained at the campground for weeks, hoping she would be found alive.Mike later hired a private detective after becoming frustrated with the progress of the investigation. He also helped establish the Laura Center, distributing millions of flyers and T-shirts carrying his daughter's photograph. Laura was among the first missing children whose pictures appeared on milk cartons.In 1986, hikers discovered fragments of a child's skull less than three miles from the campground. Subsequent forensic analysis found a greater than 99% probability that the remains belonged to a child biologically related to Mike and Patty Bradbury.Despite the findings, Mike struggled to accept that his daughter was dead. His wife Patty also continued hoping for Laura's return until her death in 2001. Mike later discovered that she had secretly written letters to their missing daughter for years."Every time I think it's behind me, it keeps coming back up," Laura's sister Emily told the Los Angeles Times, describing the emotional toll of Enders' repeated appearances.Emily's partner, Keith Hank, said Enders sometimes remains parked near the family's property for an hour or longer, playing music and whistling. He said he had contacted police several times, but officers told him they could not intervene unless her conduct became threatening or otherwise unlawful.Enders, meanwhile, has continued to insist that she is Laura. "I might drive by every day. It's my right. What do you expect me to do — sit on the other side of town knowing my father is so close?" she told the Los Angeles Times.For the Bradbury family, however, her claims remain unverified, with a DNA test still the key to establishing whether the woman is the daughter they lost in 1984.You use AI every day. articles.title: Caribbean cruise holiday turns into health scare as nearly 150 fall sick
articles.summary: Nearly 150 passengers and crew members have fallen ill aboard a Caribbean cruise ship, turning a holiday voyage into a health scare.
articles.body: Nearly 150 passengers and crew members have fallen ill aboard a Caribbean cruise ship, turning a holiday voyage into a health scare.The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is investigating the outbreak, but what triggered the illness remains a mystery.According to the CDC's Vessel Sanitation Program, 134 of the 2,936 passengers and 14 of the 1,132 crew members aboard the Caribbean Princess reported gastrointestinal symptoms during the voyage.The outbreak was reported to the agency on November 15, four days after the ship departed Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on a 12-night Caribbean and Central American cruise.The affected passengers and crew members reported vomiting and diarrhoea, according to the CDC. In response, Princess Cruises stepped up cleaning and disinfection measures across the vessel, isolated those reporting symptoms and collected stool samples for laboratory testing to identify the cause of the outbreak.A spokesperson for Princess Cruises confirmed the outbreak to NBC Miami, describing it as a "mild gastrointestinal illness"."While most guests remain unaffected, we are continuing to closely monitor the situation," the spokesperson said.The CDC said the cause of the outbreak has not yet been identified, with laboratory testing underway on samples collected from those affected. Although norovirus is a common cause of gastrointestinal outbreaks on cruise ships, health officials have not confirmed it as the source of the illness aboard the Caribbean Princess.The Caribbean Princess departed Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on November 11 for a 12-night Caribbean and Central American voyage and is scheduled to return on November 23. Operated by Princess Cruises, the vessel has a passenger capacity of 3,140 and can accommodate around 1,200 crew members. It entered service in April 2004 and measures 952 feet in length, with a gross tonnage of 112,894.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's charity gift sparked a New York school-supply drive: more than 200 fans packed 2,200 backpacks for children, while nearly 800 supporters raised close to $25,000
articles.summary: Celebrity donations can inspire a community to get involved.
articles.body: Celebrity donations can inspire a community to get involved. That is what happened in New York after Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's charitable contributions encouraged hundreds of the singer's fans to participate in a school-supply initiative. What began with a generous gift soon turned into a volunteer movement, bringing together Swifties who wanted to translate their admiration for the couple into meaningful support for children and families.Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's donation inspires fansAccording to Amny, Swift and Kelce donated a combined $26 million to various charitable organisations ahead of their July 3 wedding, with New York Cares among the beneficiaries. The nonprofit, recognised as New York City's largest volunteer organisation, subsequently organised a Swiftie-themed volunteering event on July 30.The initiative was designed to encourage fans to extend the couple's generosity through community service. New York Cares invited supporters to P.S. 20 Anna Silver on the Lower East Side, where more than 200 volunteers gathered to prepare 2,200 backpacks filled with essential school supplies for local students.According to City and Stateny, the event was part of the organisation's annual Stand with Students campaign, which aims to help children begin the academic year with the resources they need.Nearly 800 fans contribute to fundraising campaignThe impact of the celebrity couple's donation extended well beyond the volunteering event. According to City and Stateny, New York Cares noticed an increase in contributions from Swift's fanbase and developed a fundraising campaign that incorporated numbers associated with the singer's career.Donation suggestions included $13, $26, $87 and $198.90, reflecting references familiar to Swifties.Nearly 800 supporters raised nearly $25,000 using the strategy. The group sought 1,989 donors to honor Swift's birth year and 1989 album.Amny also reported that more than 700 fans had contributed over $20,000, demonstrating how the couple's charitable gesture encouraged supporters to participate financially.A Swiftie-themed event turns fandom into volunteeringThe backpack-packing event combined community service with elements of Swift's musical world. According to Amny, volunteers enjoyed the singer's music, exchanged friendship bracelets and received special event-themed pins. Exclusive T-shirts were also available to participants who made additional donations.The sold-out crowd was filled with Eras Tour fans, offering entertainment and social responsibility, City and Stateny reported.Some volunteers had never volunteered with New York Cares before. The initiative has shown how celebrity-led campaigns can attract new supporters and encourage them to participate, not just donate.New York Cares expands its mission to support studentsThe organisation plans to continue its backpack distribution efforts through additional events in September. According to Amny, its broader campaign aims to distribute 26,400 backpacks and raise $1 million.The growing participation comes at a time when community organisations are facing increasing demand for assistance. City and Stateny reported that New York Cares has been working with hundreds of partner organisations dealing with budget reductions and rising demand for services.The nonprofit is aiming to engage more than 70,000 volunteers this year and has already recorded over 66,000 participants.The initiative shows how Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's charity inspired fans to act. By combining fundraising with hands-on volunteering, New York Cares has demonstrated how a single act of generosity can inspire hundreds of others to support their communities.Images Courtesy: istock and InstagramYou use AI every day. articles.title: Buxar MP seeks increase in paddy procurement target to 60 lakh tonnes
articles.summary: Buxar MP Sudhakar Singh urges Bihar to raise 2026-27 paddy procurement target from 35 to 60 lakh tonnes, prioritise local farmers, and ensure MSP guarantee.
articles.body: Buxar: RJD MP from Buxar, Sudhakar Singh, on Friday wrote to chief minister Samrat Choudhary, demanding an increase in the state’s paddy procurement target from 35 lakh metric tonnes to 60 lakh metric tonnes for the 2026-27 kharif season.He also urged the state govt to prioritise paddy procured from local farmers to meet Bihar’s foodgrain requirements and ensure a legal guarantee for the minimum support price (MSP).In his letter, Singh said Bihar was primarily an agrarian state, with a large section of its population dependent on farming for livelihood. However, he alleged that the state’s paddy procurement policy was not adequately protecting farmers’ interests despite sufficient production.He pointed out that the Centre had fixed Bihar’s paddy procurement target at just 35 lakh metric tonnes for the 2026-27 kharif season. In comparison, the target for 2025-26 was 36.85 lakh metric tonnes, against which the state govt procured 36.79 lakh metric tonnes, achieving around 99.84% of the target, he said.He questioned the reduction in the procurement target. He also expressed doubts over the reported procurement figures.Referring to foodgrain requirements, Singh cited Centre’s data presented in Parliament, according to which 37.29 lakh metric tonnes of rice was distributed under the public distribution system (PDS) in Bihar during 2024-25. Besides, around 3.01 lakh metric tonnes of foodgrain was allocated to the state under the PM-POSHAN (midday meal) scheme in 2025-26.He questioned why Bihar continued to depend on other states for rice supplies when it had sufficient paddy production of its own. He alleged that local farmers were often forced to sell their produce at distress prices, while rice was procured from Punjab, Haryana and other states to meet the requirements of govt welfare schemes.Singh demanded that the state govt should disclose the annual quantity of rice procured from other states for PDS, PM-POSHAN and other welfare schemes, along with the share of Punjab in such supplies.The MP also criticised govt over the absence of a legal guarantee for MSP. He said the ruling alliance had promised farmers a legal guarantee for MSP during the 2025 assembly elections, but the commitment had not translated into concrete action after coming to power.He also called for opening adequate procurement centres and ensuring timely payments to farmers. articles.title: An Indiana man bought a condominium in 2020, then faced foreclosure over $5,229 in unpaid fees; after paying $9,489, he was billed $26,813, and a November 19 appeals court upheld judgment against him
articles.summary: An Indiana man who bought a condominium in 2020 has lost his appeal after a dispute over unpaid homeowners' association fees grew into a $26,813 debt,
articles.body: An Indiana man who bought a condominium in 2020 has lost his appeal after a dispute over unpaid homeowners' association fees grew into a $26,813 debt, even though he had already paid $9,489. On November 19, 2026, the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld the ruling against him and sent the case back to a lower court to decide how much he must pay for the association's legal bills.The legal fight is between Onnie James Florence Jr. and the Meridian Arch Owners Association. Florence claimed the association made several mistakes in its court case, raising questions about how his payments were handled, how court papers were delivered to him, and how his mortgage lender was involved. However, the appeals court disagreed with his claims, noting in its written decision that Florence did not show any proof that his $9,489 payment was left off his account and that he missed the deadline to fight an earlier ruling against him. According to the court decision published by Justia, the conflict started over $5,229.80 in unpaid condominium fees and eventually turned into a foreclosure case, multiple court requests, and a much bigger bill.A condominium purchase followed by unpaid feesFlorence bought a unit at Meridian Arch Condominiums in 2020. The property is run by the Meridian Arch Owners Association, which collects regular fees from owners to pay for building and community costs. According to the Indiana Court of Appeals, Florence first planned to live in the condominium with his daughter, though those plans fell through and he stayed at his home in Illinois instead. Even though he did not live there, he still had to pay the monthly fees, as unpaid bills under the association's rules can become a legal claim, or lien, on the condominium that lets the association push for foreclosure to sell the home.By May 2021, Florence owed $5,229.80 in unpaid fees, prompting the association to file a lawsuit asking the court to foreclose on its claim. The association first tried to hand the court papers to Florence in person, and when that did not work, it sent a new summons and a copy of the lawsuit by certified mail to his home in Illinois, which arrived on June 15, 2021. Florence did not answer the lawsuit or show up in court, so on September 28, 2021, the association asked the court for an automatic win, called a default judgment. According to court records, the association filed a sworn statement showing Florence owed $9,213.50 as of September 14, 2021, covering unpaid fees, late charges, collection costs, and legal bills, and the trial court agreed and ruled against him.Foreclosure proceedings beginThe association then moved to sell Florence's condominium to get the money it was owed, asking the court in November 2021 to schedule a sheriff's sale of the unit. Florence finally joined the case and asked the judge to cancel the automatic ruling against him, claiming the association had not properly delivered earlier court papers to him and had started the foreclosure too early under Indiana law. The association pushed back against those claims, stating that mailing the lawsuit and summons by certified mail to his Illinois home met all legal rules and arguing that a different Indiana law for condominium groups allowed it to start the foreclosure case when it did.In September 2022, Florence asked the court to throw out the case or merge it with a separate foreclosure lawsuit filed by his mortgage lender, CrossCountry Mortgage LLC, arguing that the association failed to tell CrossCountry about his unpaid fees before suing him despite requirements in its own rules. In October 2022, the case was moved to the same court handling the mortgage lender's lawsuit after the judge noted that both cases involved the same home, people, and money, so combining them would prevent conflicting rulings. On January 29, 2024, the court denied Florence's requests to cancel the default judgment and throw out the case.$9,489 payment did not end the disputeIn April 2024, a foreclosure order went to the sheriff to start the sale of the property, though that sale was called off after Florence paid the association $9,489. The association counted that money as a partial payment toward the existing court judgment, but it did not cover everything he owed. In September 2024, the association told the court that Florence still owed $1,922.84 on the original judgment because of interest that had piled up since the first ruling, and it also wanted to collect new unpaid fees and costs that had built up since the lawsuit began.The association stated that Florence owed another $19,368.17 in association fees, late charges, expenses, and legal bills, covering monthly fees from September 14, 2021, through December 31, 2024, plus other costs added up through August 31, 2024. At first, the judge turned down the request, explaining that the association could not simply tack years of new fees onto a lawsuit after a final ruling had already been made. After the association asked the court to set aside the old default judgment and foreclosure order so it could update its original lawsuit, the judge agreed in November 2024, and the association filed an updated lawsuit asking for the extra unpaid fees, expenses, and legal bills while officially adding CrossCountry Mortgage and an unknown resident living in the unit to the case.Court upholds $26,813 judgmentIn September 2025, the association asked the judge to decide the case without a trial, filing money records and sworn statements showing Florence owed $26,813.22 in unpaid fees, late charges, collection costs, and lawyer bills, while also showing that his $9,489 payment had been applied to his balance. The trial judge gave Florence two extra deadlines to reply to the request, said no when he asked for a third delay, and ruled in favour of the association on February 3, 2026, after Florence never filed a response. Florence then asked the judge to rethink the decision and halt a sheriff's sale set for April, claiming the association had not properly counted his earlier $9,489 payment and demanding a full, line-by-line record showing exactly where that money went, which the trial judge denied before Florence filed an appeal.In its November 19, 2026, decision, the Indiana Court of Appeals reviewed four main points Florence raised. First, the judges ruled that he had run out of time to fight the January 2024 decision that kept the original default judgment in place, as he missed the 30-day window to appeal that order under Indiana court rules. Second, the court rejected his claim that the case should be thrown out because CrossCountry was left out at the start, finding that the issue no longer mattered since the mortgage lender was later added to the updated lawsuit. Third, the judges said the association did not have to send Florence a brand-new court summons after updating its lawsuit because his lawyer was already involved in the case, meaning sending the papers to his attorney followed Indiana Trial Rule 5.Appeals court says payment was creditedTurning to the main fight over the $9,489 payment, Florence claimed the association's math ignored the money he paid in August 2024, but the appeals court pointed to the association's sworn debt record clearly listing the payment. That record stated, "The last payment was received and credited to [Florence]’s account on August 20, 2024, in the amount of $9,489[]," and the judges noted that Florence offered no proof showing that statement was wrong. He also claimed he had a right to "a verified accounting identifying each payment and its application," though the appeals court said he waited too long to bring up that point by only asking for it after losing the summary judgment, meaning he could not use it to win an appeal and leaving the court with no reason to overturn the judgment against him.The association also asked the court to make Florence pay its legal bills for the appeal, and the judges agreed, pointing to the association's governing rules allowing it to recover reasonable lawyer fees when suing to collect unpaid assessments. On November 19, 2026, the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld the lower court's ruling and sent the case back to the trial judge to calculate the exact legal fees Florence owes for the appeal. Judge DeBoer wrote the opinion, with Judges Foley and Felix concurring, keeping the $26,813.22 judgment active and letting the trial court set the final amount of extra legal fees Florence must pay to the Meridian Arch Owners Association.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iraqi forces deploy to Jurf al-Sakhar after deal with Iran-backed group
articles.summary: Iraq’s Federal Police are due to assume control of town’s newly established control headquarters.
articles.body:
Iraqi security forces have been deployed to Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the powerful Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah armed group.

Security forces arrived in the town, which sits in Babil province about 60km southwest of Baghdad and is also known as Jurf al-Nasr , on Friday.

The deployment, which is understood to have been driven by pressure from the United States and its Gulf allies, comes a day after a compromise deal was sealed that will see Kataib Hezbollah move to other areas of the country.

The government announced on Monday that it would take control of Jurf al-Sakhar after a probe raised suspicions that the group had stolen hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iraqi oil via illicit oil refineries.

It gave the group, which is believed to have thousands of trained fighters, a deadline of Friday to leave the town. However, under Thursday’s deal, they are expected to withdraw from the area within a month.

Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, has denied the allegations of stealing oil. Nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following the investigation into alleged oil smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar.

Analysts suspect the push for withdrawal is a calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into Iraq’s state apparatus. Baghdad has also come under pressure from the US to reduce Iran’s influence in the country.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has had to tread a fine line as he seeks to contain Kataib Hezbollah without triggering a confrontation.

Al-Zaidi said on Friday, as he addressed the government forces entering the town, that they were “not waging war”.

“Everyone present there are your brothers,” he told the troops, “the sons of this nation, and their blood is our blood.”

However, he insisted that his decision to restrict weapons to state control was final.

Under the compromise, a combined force comprising an Iraqi army brigade, a Federal Police battalion and an Energy Police regiment will provide protection for oil pipelines in the area.

Two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) Commission, a collection of armed groups that are part of Iraq’s official security forces, will also participate.

Lieutenant General Ahmed Hatem Hamid said on Friday that a control headquarters had been established in Jurf al-Sakhar and that the Federal Police would control the facility, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

Iraq’s Energy Police have also begun securing an oil pipeline running through Jurf al-Sakhar, INA reported.

Baghdad-based security and strategic analyst Fadel Abu Raghif told Al Jazeera that the deal for Iraqi security forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar came after lengthy and delicate talks with Kataib Hezbollah.

The agreement followed “in-depth negotiations, and after wrangling and a tug of war that lasted about two months or so,” Abu Raghif said.

Highlighting the delicacy of the situation, Esmail Qaani, the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Quds Force, had visited Iraq earlier this week to help defuse tension and seal the deal.

Kataib Hezbollah helped recapture Jurf al-Sakhar from ISIL (ISIS) and has had a large presence in the town for more than a decade.

Reporting from Babil province, Al Jazeera’s Samer Al Kobeisi said the departure of Kataib Hezbollah would allow the reopening of an area that has been closed for about 12 years, according to the government.

articles.title: Storm severely flooding Florida to disrupt holiday travel from Southeast to New England
articles.summary: The storm could even become a rare end of hurricane season tropical or subtropical storm.
articles.body: A storm flooding Florida’s Atlantic coast could hamper early Thanksgiving travel for millions as it charges up the East Coast with soaking rain and gusty winds. It could even turn into a rare end-of-season tropical or subtropical storm off the Southeast coast this weekend, but the odds of development are trending down. Either way, that designation won’t change the outcome much. Travel will be disrupted during one of the busiest periods of the holiday week. It will also continue to hammer Florida with extreme rainfall. The storm has drenched eastern parts of the state with over 16 inches of rain this week, flooding homes and forcing dozens of water rescues along the Space Coast and in Miami’s northern suburbs. A rare Level 4 of 4 high risk of flooding rain is in place from Cape Canaveral to Daytona Beach through Friday night. High risk flooding days are a big deal: They’re issued on fewer than 4% of days per year on average, but are responsible for more than 80% of all flood-related damage and 36% of all flood-related deaths, research from the Weather Prediction Center shows. Delays possible at East Coast airports Forecast models still have some notable track and timing differences for the storm’s trek up the East Coast, so confidence is lower than normal. Here’s a day-by-day look at the forecast, but expect some changes. Saturday-Saturday night: Rainfall and gusty winds will expand northward and hit parts of Georgia and the Carolinas, with rain possible into central Georgia, including Atlanta. This could cause delays at airports and flood roads, from Jacksonville, Florida, to Charleston, South Carolina, particularly closer to the coast. Beaches will also deal with erosion, high surf and coastal flooding. Sunday-Sunday night: Travel in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast will go downhill as rain spreads northward. Gusty winds could worsen travel delays in some areas. Washington, DC’s, airports could deal with rain as soon as Sunday morning, with no let up through the afternoon. That’s not a lock though, since some models steer much of the rain away from our nation’s capital. Flights from Philadelphia’s and New York’s airports should avoid any weather issues on Sunday morning, but rain and gusty winds could worsen conditions in the afternoon. Those traveling by road could contend with plenty of slowdowns too, including along the heavily traveled Interstate 95 corridor from Virginia to New York City. The rain will spread across New England by late Sunday afternoon or evening, including Boston; Hartford, Connecticut; and Providence, Rhode Island. The storm’s fast movement should prevent serious flooding, but ponding on roads is likely, especially in poor drainage areas. Rain will exit New England early Monday morning, but gusty winds could linger through the day in the storm’s wake. It’s unclear whether they will be strong enough to cause flight delays. More weather woes are possible for eastern US holiday travelers after this system departs: Another storm could impact the East Coast on Wednesday into Thanksgiving Day. Details are too fuzzy right now to be helpful, but we’ll keep updating you through the weekend. Florida’s Space Coast flooded A firehose of rainfall streaming in from the Atlantic Ocean caused floodwater to rise into “countless” homes in Brevard County, on Florida’s Space Coast, on Thursday, county spokesperson Don Walker told CNN. Rescue efforts were ongoing Friday morning, he said. More than 100 people had been rescued by the end of the day Thursday, mostly from flooded homes. The scenes are eerily similar to the historic rainfall and severe flooding that hit the area earlier this month, even flooding some of the same homes again. Jazmine Foster’s home in Melbourne, Florida, flooded on Thursday for the second time in two weeks, she told the Associated Press. She said an insurance claim filed for the earlier flood was denied. Roughly 65 homes in the Palm Bay Estates mobile home park in Brevard County were under a mandatory evacuation order Thursday after a bridge washed out and cut off the only access road, Palm Bay Fire Chief Richard Stover told CNN. Residents were evacuated by boat and brought to a temporary shelter, Stover said. The rest of the community is under a voluntary evacuation advisory, according to the city. Ten people were evacuated from other areas in Palm Bay on Thursday, Stover said. At least two water rescues were conducted, but no injuries have been reported in the city. In Rockledge, officials are going “door-to-door” to notify people in areas where evacuation is recommended due to rising water in the St. Johns River, according to a city social media post. Water rescues are ongoing, according to the city. More flooding rain is falling Friday, especially in the Level 4 of 4 high risk area. That includes parts of northern Brevard and Volusia counties, which are a bit north of the areas hardest hit on Wednesday and Thursday. Another 4 to 8 inches of rain could fall in these areas through early Saturday morning, with up to a foot in isolated places. Around 20 rescues have been conducted in Volusia County as of Friday morning, county spokesperson Michael Ryan told CNN. Water is up to several feet deep in some residential areas and has entered homes, he said. Rivers still high in the wake of flooding two weeks ago have risen even higher this week. The St. Johns River near Cocoa, Florida, surged past its record crest, set more than 70 years ago, on Thursday morning. The St. Johns river drains very slowly, so flooding in some areas could last for weeks.

articles.title: Bolton: ‘No substance’ to Trump meeting with Putin, Xi
articles.summary: Former White House national security adviser John Bolton said the trilateral meeting this week between President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping has “no substance.” “I think from what we can tell of the trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi, there is no substance to it, whatever,” Bolton said in an…
articles.body:
Former White House national security adviser John Bolton said the trilateral meeting this week between President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping has “no substance.”

“I think from what we can tell of the trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi, there is no substance to it, whatever,” Bolton said in an appearance on NewsNation’s “On Balance.”

During the talks, which occurred on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China, the world leaders were expected to touch on trade, the wars in Ukraine and Iran and rapidly evolving artificial intelligence.

Trump also met individually with Xi and Putin.

“I think if there was any content, it came in the bilateral meetings earlier today of Putin with Trump and Xi with Trump,” Bolton told host Leland Vittert. “We’ll learn more, but overall, at this point, I would rate substance level pretty close to zero.”

The trio did issue a four-point “ declaration toward peace .” The symbolic agreement says “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” It also notes that the U.S., China and Russia will conduct a dialogue on “reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”

Bolton weighed in on the vow, saying “that was Ronald Reagan’s favorite line, so I’m happy to see that revived.”

Republican lawmakers have been divided on the trilateral talks, with some backing open conversations between the superpowers and others critical of the message the conversations send to Americans and others.

“I’ve never been successful in getting inside the president’s head, but I can tell you where I am, we have to be more clear about who our friends are and who our allies are,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah), who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said earlier this month. “I would put neither of those in that category.”

Sen. Bill Hagerty (R-Tenn.), also a member of the panel, described Xi and Putin as “adversaries,” but he noted the president’s meeting with them was a “healthy thing.”

Bolton said that while Trump considers Putin and Xi as friends , it probably does not go both ways.

“I will guarantee you, that’s not how they see him,” he added.

articles.title: Magnitude 4.2 earthquake shakes Los Angeles County
articles.summary: A magnitude 4.2 earthquake shook the Commerce area of Los Angeles County and other neighboring cities in Southern California early Friday morning, according to the U.S.
articles.body: A magnitude 4.2 earthquake shook the Commerce area of Los Angeles County and other neighboring cities in Southern California early Friday morning, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. USGS first reported the earthquake as 4.2, then it upgraded it to 4.4 and downgraded again to 4.2. The quake was felt at around 3:25 a.m. and had a depth of about 9.6 miles, the USGS website said. Over 12,000 people reported having felt the shaking on the USGS’ website. According to the USGS, the earthquake’s epicenter was northwest of Commerce, a city about 7 to 8 miles from downtown Los Angeles. The USGS’ “Did You Feel It?” report showed that residents in cities like Alhambra, San Gabriel, Pasadena, Long Beach and even as far as North Hollywood and Calabasas felt the shaking. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass issued a statement on X early Friday, saying, “A 4.4-magnitude earthquake centered in Commerce impacted the L.A. region just before 3:30 AM this morning that likely woke up many Angelenos.” “While unsettling, there are no immediate reports of damage or operational impacts, including at LAX,” the statement said. “The LAFD and City teams will continue to monitor and update as needed.” Multiple earthquakes also struck near Pinnacles on Thursday night, according to the United States Geological Survey. The strongest was a 5.0 magnitude earthquake that hit at 10:40 p.m. It was centered 6.2 miles northwest of Pinnacles, according to the USGS.

articles.title: Poland says likely Russian missiles violated airspace
articles.summary: Poland’s airspace was violated by Russia overnight with two missiles and a drone, the Polish defense minister said on Friday. “There has been a violation of ​Polish airspace and an incursion by objects from the Russian Federation,” Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said at a press conference, according to a Reuters report. “There was ​a…
articles.body:
Poland’s airspace was violated by Russia overnight with two missiles and a drone, the Polish defense minister said on Friday.

“There has been a violation of ​Polish airspace and an incursion by objects from the Russian Federation,” Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said at a press conference, according to a Reuters report . “There was ​a Kh-101 missile. … In the second case, one can also speak of a missile; in the third, ⁠it was most likely a jet-powered drone.”

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the incident “an intentional provocation,” according to the report.

“Today, it is clearer than ever before ‌that Poland must ⁠participate in decisions and discussions regarding the future of Ukraine and security in Europe,” he added.

The Reuters report said the airspace violation came as Poland was holding military exercises on Friday involving the Coalition of the ​Willing , a group of countries including NATO member states that have pledged to support Ukraine in the Russia-Ukraine war, which is approaching its five-year mark.

Kosiniak-Kamysz said “these exercises, combined with the presence of defense ministers from France, the United Kingdom, and the Baltic states — ​along with eight chiefs of staff, including those from our key allies — suggest that the convergence of these events is no accident.”

He added that Poland would ask NATO for additional support in securing the alliance’s eastern flank, according to the report.

“We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend,” said NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte in a post on the social platform X . “This incident is clearly dangerous – a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. I condemn Russia’s attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine.”

Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command wrote in a post on X in the early hours of Friday that steps are being taken to verify the incident. Ground and rescue teams were dispatched to the location of possible impact to investigate.

The alleged incursion comes after Moscow and Kyiv held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months in Abu Dhabi, during which they agreed to a “large-scale” exchange of prisoners of war .

articles.title: In 1906, three Wyandot sisters guarded ancestors’ graves with their late father’s shotgun; Lyda lost her 1910 court fight, but a 1913 law saved the cemetery
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of the Wyandot sisters who courageously defended their ancestors' graves in Kansas City against government threats, leading to a historic Supreme Court case and eventual preservation efforts.
articles.body: Throughout history, women have often had decisions made for them without their consent. But once in a while, some women have refused to succumb and have held their ground. In 1906, a cemetery in downtown Kansas City, Kansas, became the site of an armed standoff, according to the Wyandot Nation of Kansas. It was led by three sisters who guarded the graves of their relatives against government regulations to sell the land and relocate the remains.According to the Wyandot Nation of Kansas, Lyda Conley, one of the three sisters, took the case to court. Her case reached the US Supreme Court in 1910, but she unfortunately lost. Three years later, in 1913, the cemetery was saved from sale when Senator Charles Curtis secured legislation that repealed the authorisation.The Wyandot National Burying Ground, also called Huron Indian Cemetery, was built in 1844 after the Wyandot people were removed from Ohio. The Wyandot Nation of Kansas recorded that the community buried its dead on high ground near the meeting of the Missouri and Kansas rivers. The Treaty of 1855 dissolved the Wyandot Nation and made its members US citizens, but permanently reserved the enclosed cemetery for burials.Sacred land in the crosshairsEfforts to sell the cemetery predated the sisters’ occupation. According to the Wyandot Nation of Kansas, Senator Preston B. Plumb labelled it a “nuisance” in 1890 and tried to sell it. The attempt failed, but local historian and businessman William Elsey Connelly later negotiated with the Wyandotte Nation of Oklahoma. Connelly was appointed the agent with a promise of a 15% commission if the deal went through.Holding the line at Fort ConleyA clause in a federal appropriations act in 1906 authorised the Secretary of the Interior to sell and move the graves, according to the Wyandot Nation of Kansas. The sisters resisted the move and occupied the grounds, KCUR reported in 2025. The Wyandot Nation of Kansas account said Lyda, Lena and Ida locked the gate, displayed a “Trespassers Beware!” sign and built Fort Conley, a six-by-eight-foot wooden guard post. The sisters defended the site by holding up their father’s double-barreled shotgun. Kansas City, Kansas, rejected an initial Interior Department offer of $75,000 in 1907, the Wyandot Nation records.Making history at the Supreme CourtIn 1907, Lyda filed a petition in the US Circuit Court for the District of Kansas, relying on the 1855 treaty’s reservation of the cemetery for burials, the Wyandot Nation of Kansas noted. She did not, however, need a lawyer in Washington to sponsor her admission to the Supreme Court Bar, since she was already a licensed attorney in Kansas and Missouri. As a result, she argued her own case and became the first Native American woman to argue before the court. According to the Wyandot Nation of Kansas, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that her Wyandot descent and relatives’ graves did not give her a legal claim to the land. The opinion treated the government’s treaty obligation as one of honour, not an enforceable legal duty.Rebuilding Fort Conley to a lifelong vigilThe ruling did not put an end to the occupation. Federal marshals demolished Fort Conley in July 1910, but the sisters rebuilt it. The Wyandot Nation recorded three rounds of demolition and reconstruction until authorities abandoned the effort. Senator Charles Curtis eventually stepped in and took up the issue.According to the Wyandot Nation of Kansas, Curtis secured a bill repealing the 1906 provision that allowed the cemetery to be sold. It was passed in February 1913. Regardless, the sisters continued to challenge work they believed threatened graves. In 1929, Lyda sat in a ditch to prevent construction of a retaining wall, the Wyandot Nation of Kansas noted. She served 10 days in jail in 1937 after she chased off people from property with a broomstick, according to the Wyandot Nation records.Lyda passed away on 28 May 1946, after being struck during a robbery, according to the Wyandot Nation of Kansas. She was buried in the cemetery. According to the National Park Service, the cemetery was entered into the National Register of Historic Places in September 1971 and became a National Historic Landmark in December 2016. The Wyandot Nation now leads the preservation work at the burial site.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
