articles.title: ‘Expel invaders’: The dangerous promises of Spain’s far-right Vox party
articles.summary: As Spain prepares to vote, Vox is campaigning on mass deportations and ‘national priority’.
articles.body:
Santiago Abascal, wearing a blue suit and tie, looks straight into the camera. His campaign poster makes three promises: giving Spanish nationals priority in access to benefits, cutting regulation and “remigration”.

“It’s common sense,” the poster of his far-right Vox party reads.

With little more than a week to go until Spain’s November 29 snap election, opinion polls put Vox in third place behind the conservative Popular Party (PP), which is leading the race, and the governing Socialist Party.

But with the Socialists’ potential allies fragmented and the PP projected to fall short of an outright majority, Vox could emerge as a kingmaker.

The party, which once struggled to win a single seat in parliament, could join a PP-led coalition or back a minority PP government from outside the cabinet.

Abascal was a regional lawmaker for the PP in the Basque Country. He left the party in 2013, accusing then-Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy of being too soft on the issue of Catalan separatism. He went on to cofound Vox.

The new party positioned itself to the PP’s right, making Spanish unity its central cause. It called for an end to the country’s system of regional autonomy and championed the idea of the “true Spaniard”, who was Catholic, Castilian-speaking and loyal to the monarchy.

Over time, the party started to adopt themes and tactics from other European far-right parties.

“At the beginning, they were the ultra-conservatives of the right, but then they started to study the handbook of the populist radical right across Europe, and they became the Spanish version of it,” said Carles Ferreira, lecturer in politics at the University of Girona.

In January 2017, Abascal made his international debut at a gathering of Europe’s far right in the German city of Koblenz alongside France’s Marine Le Pen and Frauke Petry, then-leader of the Alternative for Germany. But Vox was still a minor force at home, having won 0.2 percent of the vote and no seats in the previous year’s general election.

That October nine years ago, Catalonia held an independence referendum in defiance of Spain’s Constitutional Court. A few weeks later, the Parliament of Catalonia unilaterally declared independence, plunging the country into a constitutional crisis.

Vox, which had filed a legal complaint over the preparation for the vote, used the crisis to raise its national profile over its opposition to Catalan independence.

It worked. Just over a year later, the party made its electoral breakthrough, winning 12 seats in the regional parliament of Andalusia in southern Spain. Four months later, it entered the national parliament for the first time by winning 24 seats.

Vox had transformed from a fringe party with zero representation into a relevant political force.

The first bullet point in its manifesto calls for the “immediate expulsion of all invaders”.

Abascal has accused the Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people”.

“It may well be that the upcoming elections will be the last ones to be decided by the Spanish people,” Abascal said on Thursday on X.

He wants to ban the mass regularisation of undocumented immigrants and deport them.

His manifesto calls for “remigration”, a plan to facilitate the expulsion of people who the party says do not contribute or who rely on public benefits.

Throughout the eight-year tenure of the current government, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, according to the National Statistics Institute.

Vox is also campaigning for “national priority”, a system that would create a two-tier society in which Spanish nationals would have better access to social benefits.

Its exclusionary discourse often focuses on Muslim migrants.

“With Catalan independence no longer dominating the political debate, Vox has shifted its focus to what it calls the ‘Islamisation of Spain’ and the threat of a ‘Spanish caliphate’,” said Steven Forti, professor of contemporary history at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. “By hammering away at the issue, the party has turned it into a rallying point for voters.”

Vox draws on the idea of Hispanidad, a shared Hispanic identity, to portray Latin American migrants as culturally closer to Spaniards.

Spain has long welcomed Spanish-speaking people from Latin America. They represent the largest group of undocumented and documented foreigners in Spain, according to the Spanish think tank Funcas.

Vox’s idea of an “Iberosphere”, Forti added, invokes traditional Catholic values and a shared language and culture rooted in Spain’s colonial past. In that telling, Latin American migrants are welcome because they are “the children of our colonisation”.

On social issues, the party is staunchly conservative. It opposes abortion. Its politicians have derided LGBTQ advocacy as the work of a “lobby”, and Vox rejects treating gender-based violence as a distinct legal category, arguing that domestic violence laws should apply regardless of the victim’s sex.

It was the only party to oppose renewing Spain’s cross-party pact against gender-based violence in 2025 and has called for suspending an agreement that specifically protects women from violence by current and former partners.

Yet this year’s party manifesto is less specific about what it wants to do, calling more broadly for replacing “gender ideology” laws and strengthening police and judicial protection for women facing violence.

Traditionally, its core electoral base has been young, white and male.

In the past three years, support for Vox has risen from 13 percent to about 20 percent. Its supporters remain predominantly male, but the party has gained ground among women and voters with secondary or vocational educations.

Support has grown particularly among people aged 35 to 44 and voters under 35, including some who were too young to vote in 2023. Vox has also drawn support from people who sat out the last election.

“This trend appears linked to the party’s ability to position itself as an antiestablishment force that channels institutional disaffection and social frustration,” said Paco Camas, head of public opinion in Spain for the polling firm Ipsos. “Its message has resonated particularly with younger men facing economic uncertainty and limited opportunities for social advancement.”

When asked about their main concerns, Vox supporters cite “the government and politicians” more often than any other issue and at more than twice the rate of voters overall, Camas said.

Immigration and concerns about border management and relations with Morocco also ranked high. Housing was among their main concerns although they cited it less often than voters overall. Economic issues and job quality also ranked lower among Vox supporters than among the wider electorate.

Vox is drawing voters away from the PP. Polls suggested 15 to 20 percent of people who voted for the PP in 2023 intend to back Vox this month due to its clearer and more uncompromising positions on immigration, national identity and security.

“Some voters on the right perceive the PP as more cautious, technocratic and closely aligned with the mainstream European consensus, making Vox a more attractive option for those seeking a sharper ideological alternative,” Camas said.

articles.title: Stock investors are giving up on China
articles.summary: Chinese stocks are hitting lows for two fundamental reasons.
articles.body:
China’s closely watched CSI 300 Index has fallen 20 percent from June highs and is now officially in bear-market territory.

Chinese stocks have lost more than $3.5 trillion in value since the middle of the year. Many analysts believe that shares are still on a downward path. Morgan Stanley, for instance, sees perhaps another 15 percent drop .

“If the country is winning the future, why are its investors so glum?” asks the Economist in an article titled “China’s Stock Markets Are the Great Global Exception.” The S&P 500 in the U.S. has gained 53 percent over the last five years. In Europe, the FTSE 500 has gained 45 percent. The CSI 300 has now lost 18.5 percent in the same period.

Chinese stocks are hitting lows for two fundamental reasons. For one thing, Xi Jinping’s economic plans are not working. Second, Xi is adopting policies that reduce or even eliminate profits at listed companies, scaring away investors — especially domestic investors.

On the first point, the Chinese economy, especially from the outside, looks bright and shiny because of the country’s leadership in a number of crucial technology areas. Xi’s Made in China 2025 initiative and five-year plans — China is now in the first year of its 15th five-year plan — along with associated programs, are all tech-heavy.

“The country’s technology companies are forging ahead,” Andrew Collier, a research fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Mossavar-Rahmani Center, told me this month. He noted that corporate profits for high technology manufacturing rose 52 percent in the first nine months of this year. However, such manufacturing only accounts for roughly 6 percent of the country’s economy.

Optimists point out that the export sector is another success story. The country’s trade surplus at the end of October hit a stunning $1.04 trillion . But paradoxically, many export-oriented factories are earning only thin margins and are not doing well. This appears to be the reason why the central government, through brazen currency interventions, is slowing the rise of the renminbi . The manipulation is of course attracting criticism from the country’s trading partners.

The rest of the economy is deteriorating fast. The property sector at the end of last decade accounted for about a quarter of gross domestic product. Now, the extreme oversupply — the country has more vacant housing than its entire population of 1.4 billion people could fill — is weighing heavily on growth.

With housing prices falling, a negative wealth effect is weighing on consumption. Furthermore, Xi’s relentless drive for automation, which is producing the world’s most advanced robots, is aggravating both unemployment and underemployment.

Urban unemployment, officially pegged at 5.2 percent in September, is probably closer to 20 percent overall and much higher for the crucial 16 to 24 age cohort. Some recent college graduates are not even looking for white-collar jobs, heading straight to menial employment out of school. Gig jobs employ a stunning 44 percent of the country’s workforce.

Consumption in China accounts for only about 38 percent of GDP , one of the lowest consumption-contribution rates in the world. And from all indications consumption’s role is continuing to decline.

The central government has sporadically introduced measures to stimulate consumer spending, but they are almost always one-off programs that have no lasting effect. Xi has not implemented structural reforms that will empower consumers at the expense of state enterprises and state banks.

In sum, GDP growth, in reality, is almost certainly less than the 4.5 percent reported for the third quarter of this year.

“China’s split economy — booming in tech and slowing in everything else — is coming apart,” says economic analyst Andrew Collier.

Second, domestic investors realize that Xi is trying to take away almost all of the benefits of the country’s tech wonders. For instance, he is commoditizing China’s tech products so that they flood the world. This process, however, reduces corporate profits and therefore investor interest.

Take the initial public offering of CXMT on July 27. The memory chip firm became the most valuable Chinese public company on its first day of trading. But as Alicia Garcia-Herrero of The Wire China wrote , investors viewed the company as just “another heavily subsidized entrant” that “would now be racing to add capacity into a market already braced for a price war.”

Investors know by now that they do not control company decisions; Xi does. And he has very different goals than they have. It does not help, as Collier noted, that the “Nvidia blow-up” and related concerns “have scared away some investors in the artificial intelligence boom.”

Because of these fundamental problems, the Chinese government’s support measures have not been particularly effective this year. China’s officials every so often mount a rescue operation by the so-called “national team,” as they did in the middle of July when state-controlled firms went into the market to buy $8.9 billion of shares . But investors this year have been ignoring the government’s desire that they buy stocks.

Earlier this month, the government banned initial public offerings and large stock sales. As the Wall Street Journal’s Lingling Wei wrote , “Intervention looks more like a Band-Aid than a cure.”

Nothing seems to be working to keep stock prices high, and nothing will work until Xi stops trying to command the economy and the markets.

articles.title: Russia ‘comfortable’ with NATO-style security guarantee for Ukraine, Kushner says
articles.summary: Russia is open to Ukraine having a mutual defense pact with the U.S. and European countries, similar to NATO’s Article 5 commitment, President Trump’s son-in-law and top envoy for negotiations between Russia and Ukraine said Thursday. Speaking after a multinational gathering of Ukraine’s supporters, Jared Kushner said the Russians are open to accepting Ukraine maintaining…
articles.body:
Russia is open to Ukraine having a mutual defense pact with the U.S. and European countries, similar to NATO’s Article 5 commitment, President Trump’s son-in-law and top envoy for negotiations between Russia and Ukraine said Thursday.

Speaking after a multinational gathering of Ukraine’s supporters, Jared Kushner said the Russians are open to accepting Ukraine maintaining robust security guarantees, despite Moscow pointing to NATO enlargement as one of the triggers for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

“I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept, where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” Kushner said at a press conference in Berlin, alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and some of Ukraine’s most prominent European partners, including Germany, France and the United Kingdom.

“I think that that comes with at least, what the Russians are saying, the intention is, when this war is over, to not have another war in the future.”

Kushner said he understands there’s “a lot of skepticism and disbelief” on Russia holding to that position but said it’s important to start dialogue between Europe and the Kremlin.

“Let people discuss it. Let them hear it from each other.”

Zelensky said the best security guarantee for Ukraine, and Europe as a whole, is NATO membership.

“NATO and the EU have been and will remain the pillars of the European security architecture,” he said during the press conference.

“And we all understand that with Ukrainian strength, Ukrainian experience and Ukrainian technologies, NATO and the EU will be far more reliable defenders of the European way of life and European security.”

The press conference happened shortly after Trump called into the meeting after he held his own meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. Trump met privately with Putin and in an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Trump said in his call that Putin is serious about negotiating a peace deal with Ukraine, Politico reported .

Meanwhile, attacks continued overnight, with Ukraine targeting Russia’s Kerch bridge for the third time in three days. The massive road and rail bridge connects Russia with the occupied Crimean peninsula and is a symbol of Putin’s commitment to hold on to the territory since Russia annexed it in 2014. Ukraine’s military succeeded in damaging a portion of the bridge’s road in a major attack.

Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight Thursday to Friday included at least 98 drones and an unspecified number of Onyx anti-ship missiles, a supersonic cruise missile that has a range of nearly 200 miles, according to an analysis by the Institute for the Study of War.

Russia is escalating its attacks against Ukrainian energy infrastructure and civilian targets across the country.

The European Union ambassador to Ukraine, Katarína Mathernová, posted on social platform X that Russia was attacking Kyiv “relentlessly” Thursday, with dozens of air raid sirens and narrowly escaping a drone explosion above her head as she ran into a hotel. She said the Dutch Embassy and three other embassies have sustained damage in the attacks.

“There’s nowhere to hide from this war. russians attack everywhere. This is what Ukrainians have lived with for five years. I believe Ukraine will hold out, as it has done so far, and in the end it will prevail,” she wrote on X .

articles.title: Watch live: Trump briefs on Asia trip after Xi, Putin summit
articles.summary: President Trump will brief reporters Friday from the White House on his high-profile trip to Asia, which included an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump is expected to tout trade agreements reached with Thailand and the Philippines, as well as a symbolic peace declaration issued alongside Xi…
articles.body:
President Trump will brief reporters Friday from the White House on his high-profile trip to Asia, which included an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump is expected to tout trade agreements reached with Thailand and the Philippines , as well as a symbolic peace declaration issued alongside Xi and Putin. The summit, which garnered some scrutiny , appeared to produce few concrete breakthroughs.

The president was also expected to discuss rapidly advancing artificial intelligence with his Chinese counterpart during the visit. Concerns over AI and cybersecurity have intensified over the past week following a series of widespread technology outages .

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to join the briefing.

The event is scheduled to begin at noon EST.

articles.title: Trump calling Putin ‘my friend’ at APEC summit sparks backlash
articles.summary: When President Donald Trump called Vladimir Putin his “friend” this week, European leaders and foreign policy experts were dismayed and alarmed.
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, is wanted by the International Criminal Court on allegations of war crimes, and is accused of overseeing a yearslong campaign of election interference, sabotage and cyberattacks against the West. So when President Donald Trump pointed to the Russian leader and declared, “He’s my friend,” at the historic Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China on Thursday, the reaction from some of America’s closest European allies was one of alarm and disbelief. “God, protect us from such friends,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted to X shortly afterward. “The optics of embracing Putin and calling him a friend cause us some concern,” Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, told a news conference Thursday. He added that it posed the question of whom Trump considered a closer friend, Putin or Poland, and “if push came to shove, which friend would he choose?” Their comments came hours before Poland’s defense minister, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, accused Russia of violating the country’s airspace overnight with three objects that were probably two missiles and a drone. Elsewhere, Estonia said it would close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds for at least six months. Much of the criticism of Trump’s remark has come from Poland, historically one of Washington’s closest allies in Europe but whose officials have grown increasingly wary of Trump’s dealings with Russia. The country, which borders Ukraine, Russia and Moscow’s close ally Belarus, has long been among the most outspoken European governments warning about the threat of Russian aggression. Its security strategy also relies heavily on the United States and NATO. More broadly, the word “friend” also caused fresh alarm among other European governments, some of which are openly warning that Putin may expand his aggression beyond Ukraine and attack them, too. Ultimately, there is widespread concern that elevating Putin alongside Trump and China’s Xi Jinping will legitimize and embolden a leader whom Western governments have sought to isolate over his record of grave human rights abuses and aggression against other countries, allegations he has routinely denied. The joint declaration made by Trump, Putin and Xi after their meeting made no mention of Ukraine but condemned the International Criminal Court, which has issued a warrant for Putin’s arrest over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it was “very incomprehensible” that Trump would meet with Putin, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among those who warned against the meeting becoming a rerun of the Yalta Conference of 1945. The summit toward the end of World War II saw President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin effectively carve up occupied Germany and other parts of Europe. Others, including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, were more restrained. Asked whether Trump had “fallen for Putin’s charm offensive,” he replied that it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had “talked about the horrific loss of life, including the loss of young Russian lives, and he spoke quite passionately about that subject.” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte also defended the principle of nuclear powers meeting to pursue diplomacy. Burnham and Rutte were speaking at a meeting in Berlin of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of nearly 40 countries working to support Ukraine and provide security guarantees. They were joined by Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, the U.S. envoys tasked with brokering peace between Moscow and Kyiv. Trump called into a meeting of dozens of European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday, telling the group that Putin was ready to end the war, according to five European officials briefed on the discussions. He also encouraged the Europeans to make a deal so they can stop spending money on Ukraine and spend it on their own countries, the officials said. Kushner also mentioned the call in a post on X but said it was up to the president to reveal what he said. “Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He’s not looking to impose anything unilaterally,” Kushner said. “Any deal we do will be in close consultation with Ukraine and with Europe. That’s something that he also asked us to come here today and reassure people in that regard.” The White House did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment on the criticisms about Trump’s comment about Putin. But Trump defended his description of the Russian president in an interview with Reuters, saying that “it’s nice to have people that have 4,000 nuclear weapons as a friend as opposed to an enemy.” This is far from the first time Trump has spoken warmly about Putin, joking in 2013 about becoming his “new best friend.” Once in office, Trump said in 2018 that the pair “got on very well,” and in 2022, he described Putin’s initial moves against Ukraine as “genius” and “savvy.” In 2023 and again in 2024, Trump recounted telling Putin, “We’re friends.” However, this week was the first time Trump made the declaration to Putin’s face, in front of television cameras at one of the most hotly anticipated meetings of recent years. “It’s one thing to say in an interview, ‘We get on,’ as Trump has in the past; it’s quite another to see him crossing a room in the hotel in China with an effusive smile on his face and gushing about ‘my friend,’” said Jonathan Eyal, international director of the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It all felt very natural and very real.” The condemnation was not confined to one side of the Atlantic. In the United States, Democrats were openly scathing. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York called Trump’s words “embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” while Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, described Trump’s “friend” as a “murderous war criminal.” Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona said: “Putin is not my friend. He’s not your friend. He’s not a friend of this country, and when the president of the United States refers to him in that way, it emboldens him.” Republicans were more circumspect. Sen. Rick Scott of Florida called Putin a “thug” but acknowledged that Trump needed to work with him. Bill Browder, a British American financier who spearheaded the international campaign for Russian sanctions and has become one of Putin’s most prominent critics, also described his “revulsion and disgust” at hearing Trump’s words. “He’s a guy who’s a geopolitical menace, and he should not get any kind of respect, let alone from the American head of state,” Browder told NBC News in a telephone interview. “To be elevated to the top table with genuine superpowers is an unbelievable symbolic position to sit in.” When asked about Trump’s comment at the end of the news conference following the “Coalition of the Willing” meeting in the German capital, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy only shrugged and walked offstage.

articles.title: Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close New York’s Rikers Island jail by 2032
articles.summary: The plan would replace the jail complex with four smaller jails and reduce the number of people behind bars.
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled a plan to close the notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, setting out how his administration hopes to shut down a facility long criticised for violence, overcrowding and poor sanitation.

The plan, released on Friday, proposes closing the jail five years after a deadline of August 2027 that was set under then-Mayor Bill de Blasio.

With less than a year to go, the four smaller jails in four New York boroughs that are meant to replace Rikers are still under construction.

The jail complex mostly holds people awaiting trial rather than serving sentences after conviction.

“For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane,” said Mamdani in a statement.

“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers,” he said.

How does Mamdani plan to close Rikers Island?

The mayor’s strategy involves reducing the number of people held at Rikers from 6,700 to no more than 4,100 by expanding alternatives to detention, restoring online bail payments, investing in programmes that aim to reduce repeat offending, and shortening court delays.

Court delays can leave people “detained for years in what is essentially legal purgatory”, said Mamdani at a news conference on Friday. The city plans to set up a task force to deal with bottlenecks and improve how agencies share evidence.

Under the new timeline, the first replacement jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, with the rest completed by 2032. The city plans to also make hospital beds available for people in custody who have serious mental health or medical needs.

“Any family member of someone held at Rikers will tell you how isolating that jail is, how it can take hours to visit a loved one,” Mamdani said, adding that the new jails would be closer to courts and public transport, and would help integrate imprisoned New Yorkers back into the city.

Rikers Island, near LaGuardia airport in New York’s East River, opened in 1932 and has long faced criticism over violence, abuse, and unsanitary conditions, with campaigners pushing for its closure for over a decade.

The facility has been tied to cases like that of Kalief Browder, who spent three years there awaiting trial before the charges against him were dismissed. He died by suicide in 2015 aged 22, two years after his release.

City lawmakers voted to close Rikers in 2019, and Mamdani has blamed the city’s inability to meet the 2027 deadline to build the replacement jails on the previous administration.

Once the jail closes, Mamdani said he wants the island to be used for renewable energy and projects to help the city withstand the effects of climate change.

“Our hope is that the new Rikers Island will be unrecognisable,” he said.

articles.summary: President Trump, fresh from his trip to Asia, is briefing reporters on his trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. articles.body:
President Trump, fresh from his trip to Asia, is briefing reporters on his trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also joined the president for Friday’s briefing.

Trump touted the rare summit as “Great and Highly Consequential” in a post online following the meeting. Earlier Thursday, the trio announced the talks yielded a symbolic “declaration toward peace.”

Meanwhile, Senate Republicans are increasingly at odds over the Trump administration’s push for a $350 billion Pentagon funding package . Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) warned that the reconciliation process could expose deep divisions within the GOP over Medicaid cuts enacted last year.

Some lawmakers are eager to revisit the healthcare reductions, while others fear reopening the debate could unravel key provisions of Trump’s signature tax law. Hill Insiders can learn more here .

On Thursday, Senate Republicans blocked another war powers resolution that would restrict further military operations in Iran. The upper chamber did advance the bipartisan permitting reform bill though, sending it to the House.

A federal district court in Virginia will also hear arguments Friday on a lawsuit seeking to prevent the construction of Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch. The hearing comes two days after a federal judge extended the block on construction.

Trump will host a reception in the afternoon and hold signing time. First lady Melania Trump, whose docuseries premiered late Thursday on Prime Video, will attend an arrival ceremony for the White House Christmas tree.

articles.title: Sara Bareilles performed at a New York fundraising gala on November 17 that raised more than $1.8 million from over 500 guests, supporting local journalism, public radio and cultural programmes across the city
articles.summary: Grammy-winning singer-songwriter Sara Bareilles performed at a major fundraising gala in New York City on Tuesday evening, helping raise more than $1.8
articles.body: Grammy-winning singer-songwriter Sara Bareilles performed at a major fundraising gala in New York City on Tuesday evening, helping raise more than $1.8 million (£1.42 million) for independent journalism and cultural programmes. The event took place on 17 November at Gotham Hall in Manhattan. More than 500 guests, including well-known figures, donors and civic leaders, attended the gathering in support of New York Public Radio (NYPR), the parent organisation of WNYC and WQXR. According to NYPR's announcement on 18 November, the money raised will support local news reporting, cultural projects and educational programmes across the city.Speaking to the audience, Bareilles highlighted the importance of public radio in bringing communities together and providing reliable information. "In a world that often feels fragmented, public radio is a lifeline that brings us together through storytelling, music, and essential local news," said Bareilles, who is known for songs such as 'Brave' and for writing the Broadway musical 'Waitress'. "I am so honoured to be here tonight to celebrate and support the work they do every single day to keep our city informed and inspired." The money raised will support NYPR's work in independent journalism and cultural programming. The organisation provides non-commercial news and entertainment to millions of listeners across the tri-state area and beyond.A night for New York’s media landscapeThe annual gala is New York Public Radio's biggest fundraising event. This year's gathering was organised by a committee of NYPR trustees and supporters who wanted to help maintain the organisation's work across its different services. The event took place at a difficult time for many media organisations across the United States, with several outlets facing financial pressure. The strong support from New York donors showed the importance many people place on public media, particularly its work in fact-based reporting and the arts. According to NYPR's official announcement, donations will support several areas of its work. These include the WNYC newsroom, investigative journalism teams and talk shows. The funds will also help WQXR continue its classical music broadcasts and support arts-related activities.Investing in independent journalismLaFontaine E. Oliver, President and CEO of New York Public Radio, praised the donors for helping the organisation continue its work. He said their contributions would directly support its ability to provide independent news and cultural programmes to the public. "The incredible generosity of our community tonight ensures that New York Public Radio can continue to provide the independent journalism and unparalleled cultural programming that New Yorkers rely on," Oliver said in a statement. "This support strengthens our ability to hold power to account, tell important local stories, and amplify diverse voices across our city and region."In recent years, NYPR has worked to expand its online presence and improve its investigative reporting. Both areas require significant funding, and the money raised at the gala will help the organisation continue these efforts. The fundraising event also highlighted the work of WQXR, which is New York's only all-classical music radio station. Part of the money will help support new musical talent, develop educational programmes and maintain the station's place in the city's classical music community.The role of public media in civic lifeNew York Public Radio is a non-profit organisation supported by its listeners. Unlike commercial media companies, it does not depend mainly on advertising revenue. Its work focuses on serving the public and covering issues that matter to local communities. Speakers and hosts at the gala highlighted the importance of reliable local journalism in a healthy democracy. NYPR regularly reports on issues affecting different neighbourhoods across New York, including stories that may receive less attention from larger media organisations.Through its news coverage, music and cultural programmes, the organisation aims to help people stay informed and take part in their communities. The strong fundraising result suggests that its work continues to receive support from listeners and donors. NYPR has not yet published a detailed breakdown of how the £1.42 million equivalent raised at the event will be divided between its different services. However, officials assured guests that the money would be used carefully across the organisation's platforms.The evening ended with an acoustic performance by Sara Bareilles. Her appearance brought the fundraising event to a close, with guests celebrating both her music and the support raised for New York's media and cultural organisations. articles.title: An Australian data centre with Anthropic as its anchor tenant drew 595 objections or requests for delay and just two supportive submissions, as people raised concerns about electricity, water, traffic and noise
articles.summary: A proposed data centre in regional Queensland, Australia, has received overwhelming opposition from residents, with 595 submissions objecting to the
articles.body: A proposed data centre in regional Queensland, Australia, has received overwhelming opposition from residents, with 595 submissions objecting to the project or requesting a delay, compared with only two in support. The figures were disclosed in a filing lodged on behalf of developer Zerra DC, as reported by Reuters on November 20. The proposed Western Downs Digital Park, about 250 kilometres west of Brisbane, is expected to become one of Australia's largest computing facilities, with artificial intelligence company Anthropic signed as its anchor tenant.The filing recorded nearly 600 public submissions, including one neutral response. It also acknowledged that many residents had raised concerns about the project's potential effects on water resources, electricity supply, noise, roads and local housing. The development has become a major point of debate over the infrastructure demands of large-scale artificial intelligence operations and the impact they could have on communities hosting them.Residents raise concerns over power, water and roadsAccording to the filing, a significant number of submissions raised concerns about the scale of the development and its possible effects on the surrounding region. Objectors questioned how much water the facility would require, whether its electricity demand could affect power prices and supply, and whether construction traffic would damage local roads. Others raised concerns about noise and additional pressure on housing.The project is planned on farmland in the Western Downs region. Its proposed IT capacity is 1.44 gigawatts, which would make it one of the largest data centre developments in Australia. Around one-third of the submissions came from people living within 200 kilometres of the proposed site, according to the filing.The timing of the objections is also notable. The project had received five objections in the month before Anthropic was named as its tenant on September 15. Most of the remaining submissions arrived between that announcement and November 11, when the local government closed the public consultation period.Developer outlines water and electricity plansZerra DC has said it takes the community's concerns seriously and that the submissions show residents want a greater say in how the development proceeds. The company said it was expanding its community engagement and planned to report on changes requested by the public.On its official Western Downs Digital Park website, the developer describes the proposal as a master-planned digital and energy precinct with up to four phases of artificial intelligence-ready data centres. The project is being developed and will be operated by Zerra DC, with Australian Data Centres and Macquarie Capital serving as investors in the project.The developer says the facilities will use air-cooled technology rather than water-based evaporative cooling. The developer has proposed using processed water from nearby gas operations during construction, subject to agreements and approvals. During operations, it plans to rely primarily on rainwater harvesting and on-site recycling, rather than regular groundwater extraction.For electricity, the developer says the project will draw power from the national electricity market and procure a combination of supply from existing Queensland generators and new generation. The developer has also said it will cover the full cost of connecting to the grid, including any network upgrades required for the project. However, this commitment does not establish that the development will have no wider effect on electricity supply or prices.Anthropic lease puts project in spotlightThe proposed development is a major investment in regional digital infrastructure. The developer's website describes Anthropic's agreement as a long-term lease commitment, although the project remains subject to planning and regulatory approvals. An earlier report by ABC News described the proposal as a $32 billion development comprising four data centres. It reported that the first facility had been leased by Anthropic for potential use as early as 2027. The report also outlined the developer's plans for air cooling and rainwater collection, alongside questions from local residents and energy experts about the project's demands on the electricity system.The opposition comes amid wider debate in Australia about the resources required by data centres supporting artificial intelligence. Reuters noted that other projects have also faced resistance, including a proposed Sydney development that Goodman Group scrapped after public opposition and a Melbourne project by NextDC that was delayed amid concerns about energy use.For the Western Downs Digital Park, the public submissions do not determine the outcome of the planning application. The proposal is still being assessed by the Western Downs Regional Council. However, the response highlights the challenge facing developers seeking to build large AI infrastructure projects while addressing local concerns about their environmental, economic and practical effects.You use AI every day.
